Overview

Evidence cut-off 2026-10-29 · Scope: Chapter 2 (Freedom of movement for workers) and Technology and AI recommendations; comparator step on three issues

Overall assessment Agent synthesis, validated at G7

This overview lists the 48 reform issues identified for North Macedonia in RUN-2026-01: 14 under Chapter 2 (Freedom of movement for workers) and 34 under the cross-cutting technology and AI theme. All values shown are judgements validated by the analyst at G6. Nineteen issues are rated High priority (4 in Chapter 2 and 15 in the technology theme, one of them set to High by the analyst at G6), 24 Medium and 5 Low. The dominant pattern is persistence: 33 of 48 issues have a persistent direction of travel, and no Chapter 2 issue is judged to be improving. Five technology issues are improving: electronic public procurement tools, electronic communications law, the cybersecurity framework, electronic identification and trust services law, and customs IT systems. Where the improvement is in law only, the issue briefs say so. Two technology issues are worsening and one is new. No issue's gap is closed: 20 gaps are open, 27 partly addressed, and one, on third-country workers, cannot be judged on the evidence. Most issues are of Medium tractability. The comparator pilot covered three High priority issues: nationality discrimination in access to employment (RI-FMW-001), the underused interoperability platform (RI-TEC-028) and the national e-services portal (RI-TEC-036).

RI-FMW-001 · North Macedonia

Nationality discrimination in access to employment

Chapter 2

The law governing access to the labour market does not give EU workers equal treatment with nationals, for example by treating them as any other foreigner or reserving private sector posts for nationals.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its law on access to the labour market with the EU acquis, in particular on non-discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers in all sectors, so that by accession EU citizens can work there without restrictions such as work permits. The Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners is in practice, and it was amended in 2021 and in April 2025, but the 2025 amendment only renames ministries and bodies, and further amendments on the employment of foreigners are listed only as proposed in machine-translated government reports. The Commission states that the law does not distinguish EU citizens from other foreigners and that some private sector posts are reserved for nationals. North Macedonia points to the ban on nationality discrimination in the Law on Labour Relations, which is adopted but not shown in application. No outcome has been assessed. The gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    31 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    The core recommendation has barely changed. From 2020 to 2022 the Commission asked the country to continue adapting the legal framework on access to the labour market, in particular on non-discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers. From 2023 it added the words "in all sectors", and in 2025 "adapt" became "align". Each report from 2020 to 2024 found no progress, and the 2025 report found no legislative developments. The February 2025 screening report made the requirement more concrete: partial alignment, an end-point at accession with no work permit or residence permit for EU workers, and exclusion of EU citizens from the annual foreign worker quotas. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

    15 items, 2015 to 2026 on what the country has done.

    • Law Amending the Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners 2025 ◐Adopted
    • Proposed amendments on the employment of foreigners ○Proposed
    • Law on Labour Relations ◐Adopted

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ■Unresolved gap Open Validated

    What remains is equal treatment of EU workers in the law on access to the labour market, including an end to posts in private companies reserved for nationals. The foreigners law is itself the barrier, the 2025 amendment only renames bodies and the further amendments are only proposed with unknown content (all statuses are proposals; the two government items are machine translated, so capped at Medium), while the country's general ban on nationality discrimination is its own account and does not close the gap. The Commission's statement that the law makes no EU distinction conflicts with the country's account on quotas, which is reported and partly explained under RI-FMW-002.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    Sub-area wording on access to the labour market, which matches this issue, says no progress in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, and the 2025 report says there were no legislative developments. The 2025 screening finding of partial alignment is a first assessment of that kind and does not show a change.

    No evidence recorded for this step in this run.
  6. Comparator evidence Stated
    CMP-0001

    Croatia

    What was done: Croatia wrote equal treatment and permit-free work for EU nationals into its 2011 Aliens Act, commencing on accession, and the Commission recorded completed legal alignment in 2012; no extracted item links the two. The extracted items give no data on what happened to EU workers in practice.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia's stated position is a foreigners law that makes no distinction for EU citizens, with a requirement that runs to the time of accession and further amendments of unknown content. If it chose to, North Macedonia could use a general foreigners law to carry a separate regime for EU nationals, adopted before accession, as Croatia did. Whether commencing that regime on accession would be enough is untested: the case does not show that this design earned the Commission's rating or that EU workers then had equal access, and it says nothing on reserved private sector posts.

    ▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

    CMP-0002

    Montenegro

    What was done: Montenegro adopted a separate regime for EU nationals in its foreigners law in December 2025, with named clauses applying only from accession, and Chapter 2 was provisionally closed in June 2026; no extracted item links the two. What closed the benchmark is not public, and there are no measured results yet, only an uncorroborated Government claim of improved procedures.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: the Commission says North Macedonia's foreigners law does not distinguish EU citizens from other foreigners and that it needs to ensure unrestricted access by accession. On quotas its sources conflict: the Commission asks for EU citizens to be excluded, while the country's own account says quotas do not apply to them following a reciprocity agreement, as validated judgement JDG-009552 reports. If North Macedonia chose this route, it could write an equal-treatment clause and a quota carve-out into its foreigners law, as Montenegro did about six months before the chapter closed, with at least the carve-out deferred to accession. The sequence is suggestive only: it does not show that this law met the benchmark, that deferral was accepted, or that anything changed for EU workers.

    ▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

    CMP-0003

    Serbia

    What was done: Serbia reported in the 2015 screening report that its 2014 law contains a clause giving EU citizens free access on accession, and it later amended the law to simplify permits, but the Commission still says EU citizens are covered by the rules for third-country nationals. This is a stalled case, and no extracted item says why.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Serbia is a stalled case with a closely similar Commission finding in different words, covering the permit regime but not reserved private sector posts. It suggests that if North Macedonia amended its foreigners law only to simplify permits for all foreigners, this could earn a chapter-level finding of limited progress while the gap the Commission names remains: permit simplification was one of two stated grounds in each year, with EURES preparations in 2024 and electronic data exchange in 2025. Serbia also reported a general ban on nationality discrimination in the same report that found misalignment, as North Macedonia does now in its own account. It cannot show why the gap persisted or whether a clause deferred to accession is enough.

    ◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

  7. Lesson Assessed

    Three points recur across the cases. First, two countries wrote rules for EU nationals as a separate regime inside a general foreigners law, giving equal treatment with nationals and work without a permit: Croatia in its 2011 Aliens Act and Montenegro in its December 2025 amendments. This answers the same legal mechanism the Commission names for North Macedonia, whose law treats EU citizens the same as other foreigners. Second, both countries deferred some or all of these provisions to accession, and no case shows that deferral is enough: Croatia's rating is not attributed to the Act, Montenegro's deferred clauses cannot yet have been applied, and Serbia reported a clause of this kind in 2015 while the Commission still found misalignment in 2015 and partial alignment in 2024 and 2025. Third, Serbia suggests that simplifying permits for all foreigners can earn a finding of limited progress while the difference in treatment the Commission names remains. No case addresses posts in private companies reserved for nationals, which is part of North Macedonia's gap. Agent synthesis, validated at G6b

    No evidence recorded for this step in this run.
  8. Priority Assessed

    ▲Priority High Validated

    A key recommendation on non-discrimination against EU workers is repeated in the 2020 to 2025 reports, and equal access is central to the chapter. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found in the evidence.

    ◆Tractability Medium Validated

    The change is legal and within the government's control, and the same law was amended in 2021 and 2025. Against that, six reports record no alignment and the requirement runs to the time of accession, so there is no evidence of past progress.

  9. Policy option Assessed
    RI-FMW-001Internal draft Agent synthesis

    Option 1: Write equal treatment for EU nationals into the law, as a distinct regime

    Details
    Comparator it draws on
    Croatia, Montenegro
    Gap it addresses
    the law on access to the labour market does not give EU workers equal treatment with nationals.
    Rationale
    Croatia (relevance High) and Montenegro (relevance High) each placed EU nationals in a separate regime within their foreigners law, with equal treatment and permit-free work.
    Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
    Conditional: the design answers the same mechanism, but neither case shows that it earned the Commission's assessment or changed access for EU workers.
    Problem it targets
    legal or regulatory gap (MEC-01).
    Preconditions
    North Macedonia has a separate law on employment of foreigners, so the regime would need to cover that law as well as any residence rules, not one act only; the provisions to be changed would first need to be listed.
    Risks
    drafting a clause that the Commission does not accept as full alignment, as in Serbia; leaving the reserved private sector posts untouched, since no case covers them.
    Responsible actor
    the Government, through the ministry responsible for the law on employment of foreigners, now the Ministry of Economy and Labour, with adoption by the Assembly.
    RI-FMW-001Internal draft Agent synthesis

    Option 2: Settle the commencement design early, rather than assume that deferral to accession is enough

    Details
    Comparator it draws on
    Croatia, Montenegro, Serbia
    Gap it addresses
    the requirement that EU citizens can access the labour market without restrictions by accession.
    Rationale
    all three cases. Croatia and Montenegro deferred provisions to accession, and Serbia reported a deferred clause while misalignment findings continued.
    Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
    Conditional: this is a warning drawn from the tool's reading of three cases, not a tested lesson, and what closed Montenegro's benchmark is not public.
    Problem it targets
    legal or regulatory gap (MEC-01).
    Preconditions
    a clear view, through the negotiation process, of which provisions must apply before accession and which may start on accession.
    Risks
    a law that is aligned on paper but leaves EU workers inside the foreigner regime until accession, which may not satisfy a closing benchmark.
    Responsible actor
    the Government and its negotiating structures, with the ministry responsible for labour.
    RI-FMW-001Internal draft Agent synthesis

    Option 3: Do not treat permit simplification or the general non-discrimination rule as the answer

    Details
    Comparator it draws on
    Serbia
    Gap it addresses
    the Commission's finding that EU citizens are treated as any other foreigner. North Macedonia points to the reference to nationality discrimination in its Law on Labour Relations, but the validated gap judgement finds that this, being the country's own account, does not close the gap.
    Rationale
    Serbia (relevance Medium) simplified permits for all foreigners and reported a general non-discrimination clause, while the Commission still found that EU citizens were covered by the rules for third-country nationals.
    Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
    Conditional: the point rests on the Commission's wording, not on a stated lesson, and Serbia's reasons for its slow pace are not in the evidence.
    Problem it targets
    legal or regulatory gap (MEC-01).
    Preconditions
    any permit reform would be paired with an explicit provision on EU nationals, as in Option 1.
    Risks
    reporting progress on procedures while the gap the Commission names remains.
    Responsible actor
    the ministry responsible for labour, and the Employment Service Agency where permit procedures change.

    Related step outside the comparator evidence. Removing posts in private companies reserved for nationals is part of the gap but is not covered by any case, so no option is drafted on it here. The laws that reserve these posts are not identified in the evidence, and identifying them is an open question for the next run.

RI-TEC-012Validated

Electronic communications regulator independence and market oversight weak

Technology and AI Digital infrastructure and connectivity

EU The electronic communications regulator lacks guaranteed independence in appointments and funding and sufficient capacity, and competitive safeguards in a concentrated telecom market are not applied. 24 EU requirements, 2020 to 2026.

→Direction of travel Persistent■Unresolved gap Open▲Priority High◆Tractability Medium

Strengthening the independence and capacity of this regulator was a key Commission recommendation in every report from 2021 to 2025, and an independent regulator is central to the digital infrastructure theme. The 2026 key recommendation names only the media regulator and the public service broadcaster, and the call for the Agency for Electronic Communications to increase its independence moves to body text, so High rests on five earlier reports and a requirement still stated in 2026; it is not a Reform Agenda step, and if the 2027 report also leaves it out of the key recommendations, Medium would fit. The competition part is supported by repeated but less prominent findings and did not drive the rating.

RI-TEC-012 · North Macedonia

Electronic communications regulator independence and market oversight weak

Technology and AI Digital infrastructure and connectivity

The electronic communications regulator lacks guaranteed independence in appointments and funding and sufficient capacity, and competitive safeguards in a concentrated telecom market are not applied.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to strengthen the independence and capacity of the electronic communications regulator and to improve competition in the telecom sector. Parliament adopted a new Law on Electronic Communications in June 2025, which states that the Agency is independent, but that is a legal provision and no item confirms its application. The Commission reports that parliament dismissed all five members of the regulator's commission in September 2024. On competition, machine-translated regulator reporting states that a spectrum tender received a single compliant bid, with the award decision postponed to 12 January 2026, and the Commission says a new operator took part in a tender. Success and attribution for that tender are insufficient_evidence, and the mobile market remains concentrated. The validated assessment is that the gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    24 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    The Commission's concern about the regulator's independence recurs in nearly unchanged terms from 2020 to 2025: concerns over appointments in 2020 and 2021, concerns over independence in 2022, calls to ensure full independence in 2023 and 2024, and a call to bolster independence in 2025. The key recommendation on the regulator's independence and capacity appears in every report from 2021 to 2025. On competition, the wording moves from no relevant developments in 2020 and 2021, to a market mainly shared by two operators in 2023, to a new operator taking part in a tender in 2025. In 2025 and 2026 the Commission adds points on the new law, including concerns about its provisions on financing the Operational and Technical Agency. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  2. Country response Stated

    8 items, 2022 to 2026 on what the country has done.

  3. Implementation Assessed

    2 proposed · 1 in practice

    • Law on Electronic Communications 2025 adopted (proposed)
    • 5G spectrum assignment ●In practice
    • Public tender for radio frequency bands 700 MHz, 1800 MHz and 3.x GHz ○Proposed
    • Third mobile network operator ○Proposed
  4. Outcome Assessed
    • Public tender for radio frequency bands 700 MHz, 1800 MHz and 3.x GHz: ∅Success Insufficient evidence ∅Attribution Insufficient evidence

    Adoption is not success.

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ■Unresolved gap Open Validated

    The 2026 report again asks the Agency for Electronic Communications to increase its institutional independence, and the 2025 law's statement that the Agency is independent is a legal provision, not evidence of practice. The competition part has moved, as a new operator was licensed in January 2026 as the third mobile network operator after a tender with a sole bidder, although no item yet shows it operating or its effect on a market held mainly by two operators. What remains is independence shown in appointments and practice, the third operator's actual entry, and resolving the financing provisions for the Operational and Technical Agency, on which the Commission and the country disagree and which concern that agency and not the regulator itself; the gap stays open because the requirement repeated in 2026 concerns independence, on which nothing has changed.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    Commission concern about the regulator's independence recurs in nearly unchanged terms in each report from 2020 to 2025, with no recorded improvement, so the default applies; in September 2024 parliament dismissed all five commission members, which the source reports without saying what it meant for independence. The chapter scale was not decisive. The competition part has moved a little, from no relevant developments in 2020 and 2021 to a market still shared by two operators in 2023 and a new operator taking part in a frequency tender in 2025, so the two parts of this issue do not move together.

  6. Comparator evidence Stated

    No comparator analysis for this issue in this run.

  7. Lesson Assessed

    No comparator analysis for this issue in this run.

  8. Priority Assessed

    ▲Priority High Validated

    Strengthening the independence and capacity of this regulator was a key Commission recommendation in every report from 2021 to 2025, and an independent regulator is central to the digital infrastructure theme. The 2026 key recommendation names only the media regulator and the public service broadcaster, and the call for the Agency for Electronic Communications to increase its independence moves to body text, so High rests on five earlier reports and a requirement still stated in 2026; it is not a Reform Agenda step, and if the 2027 report also leaves it out of the key recommendations, Medium would fit. The competition part is supported by repeated but less prominent findings and did not drive the rating.

    ◆Tractability Medium Validated

    The two parts differ. Independence looks hard, because it depends on appointments by parliament and exposure to political interests, and six years of reports record no progress, while competition looks more realistic because a tender has reached a compliant bid. That tender rests on one bidder and was held up by elections and a missing opinion from the anti-corruption commission, as machine-translated regulator reporting states, so Medium is a blend that would not hold if the issue were split.

  9. Policy option Assessed

    No policy options for this issue in this run.

The Commission asks North Macedonia to establish a system for appointing EURES members and partners and to give private employment agencies access to it, and its key recommendation asks the country to strengthen the Employment Service Agency and align legislation and good practice with the EURES and European Labour Authority regulations. At screening, North Macedonia stated that the Agency will be the main EURES implementing body and National Coordination Office, and that it foresees an EU-funded analysis of harmonisation needs and stronger Agency capacity. All four responding measures remain proposed, and the Commission reported no developments on EURES in November 2025. There is no outcome evidence. The Commission asks North Macedonia to negotiate and conclude bilateral social security coordination and healthcare insurance agreements with EU Member States and to put in place administrative measures to prepare for accession. The ministry lists agreements it describes as in force and applied, including with 13 Member States, but this list is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence and gives no case data. Negotiations with Italy, the USA and Greece began in 2023, yet the Commission reports no new agreements signed in any year from 2021 to 2025. RI-TEC-004 · North Macedonia

Core e-government building blocks missing

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services Digitalisation of government or economic activity Interoperability and electronic systems

Shared systems that every institution needs to work digitally, such as a single document management system, legal and technical arrangements for electronic archiving, a digital mailbox and shared administrative information systems, are missing or little used.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to put in place the basic systems that e-government needs, and the Reform Agenda ties payments to three steps: legislation allowing electronic documents to be archived, data storage infrastructure with an e-platform for record keeping and archival work, and a single document management system for all central institutions. Parliament adopted the Law on Archival Material and Archival Activity in June 2025 and the Commission considers that step achieved, but the law applies only from 1 June 2026 and its by-laws remain proposed. The Commission's technical checks found the document management system only partially operational, and the government reports that 22 institutions use a very small part of it, on machine-translated figures. The Commission's statement that adoption facilitates e-government is judged too early to show success. The validated assessment is that the gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    8 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    In 2020 and 2023 the Commission's wording in this area concerns the human resources management information system, whose use it says increased but could be further exploited. In July 2023 the Commission states more broadly that basic systems such as a digital mailbox need to be put in place to advance e-government. From October 2024 the requirement becomes concrete and conditional: the Reform Agenda sets three payment conditions on archiving legislation, storage infrastructure with an archival e-platform, and a single document management system for all central institutions. In October 2025 the Commission explains the purpose, stating that the legal framework and a complete document management system will let institutions exchange and store documents electronically without printing. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    Of the three Reform Agenda requirements, the archiving law is adopted and applies from June 2026, and the Commission reports a central document management system in use by 44 institutions by the end of June 2026, which is short of the single system across all central institutions that the Reform Agenda requires. No 2026 item for the country reports the storage and record-keeping platform, the digital mailbox or the by-laws, or says whether the 2026 deadlines were met. What remains is the platform, the digital mailbox, the by-laws and extending the document system to all central institutions.

    ↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

    The public administration rating is context only, but the Commission attributes its some progress in 2026 partly to the upgraded document management system, and it records a central document management system launched and in use by 44 institutions by the end of June 2026, which is a change in use and not only in law. Earlier figures were 21 institutions in 2022 and 22 in 2025, from machine-translated national sources capped at Medium, and the 2026 report calls the system new, so the counts may not measure the same system; the direction is clear but its size is uncertain. The Reform Agenda requires the system across all central institutions, so this is improving and not largely resolved.

RI-TEC-011 · North Macedonia

Electronic communications law not aligned with EU rules

Technology and AI Digital infrastructure and connectivity

The law on electronic communications is not fully aligned with the European Electronic Communications Code, the Gigabit Infrastructure Act and related rules on cost reduction, spectrum, roaming and open internet access.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its electronic communications law with the European Electronic Communications Code and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act, and ties adoption of an aligned law to a Reform Agenda payment. A new Law on Electronic Communications was adopted in June 2025 and amended in December 2025, with application from 1 June 2026 and by-laws due within 15 months. Both measures are validated as adopted, not as applied. The Commission found the Reform Agenda step not achieved in 2025 and 2026 while the country considers it achieved, a confirmed conflict. Separately, the Regional Roaming Agreement is judged to have worked, on Commission statements without price data. What remains is closing the gaps with the Gigabit Infrastructure Act in two laws and adopting the by-laws. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

    55 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    From 2020 to 2022 the Commission repeated that the Law on Electronic Communications needed further alignment with the EU acquis. From 2022 its recommendations named the Electronic Communications Code and the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive, and in 2023 it found no progress. In 2024 the Reform Agenda made adoption of a new law aligned with the Gigabit Infrastructure Act a payment condition. After the 2025 law, the Commission found significant harmonisation gaps, and in May 2026, after the December amendments, it found alignment only partially achieved and asked for amendments to both the electronic communications and construction laws.   5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The 2026 report finds the Law on electronic communications amended in December 2025 and June 2026 to align with the Electronic Communications Code and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act and fully applicable from June 2026, and the Law on construction amended in December 2025 to harmonise with several provisions of the Gigabit Infrastructure Act, and its Chapter 10 key recommendations no longer name the Code or the Act. Against that, the Commission's May 2026 payment assessment, made before the June amendments, considered the Reform Agenda step not achieved while the country considered it achieved, and no later item states that alignment is complete or reports the by-laws adopted within the law's 15-month deadline. What remains is confirmation that the harmonisation gaps in both laws are closed and the adoption and application of the by-laws, so the improvement shown so far is legal.

    ↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

    Commission wording that the law needs further alignment repeated from 2020 to 2022, and the matching sub-area wording in 2023 was no progress, but the wording then changed: the 2025 assessment found significant gaps after the new law, and the 2026 assessment found alignment partially achieved after the December 2025 amendments. The chapter-wide limited progress of 2024 is context only and was not decisive. Sources conflict on the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive: the Commission said in 2024 that the country was yet to align, while the country's reported view in the screening is full alignment, and this is not resolved here.

The roaming and net neutrality parts of the issue are largely positive and do not drive this rating.

    ◆Tractability Medium Validated

    The mechanisms are legal alignment and implementing rules, led by one ministry with the regulator and parliament, and a new law and amendments were adopted in 2025, which favours progress. Against that, the Commission assessed the Reform Agenda step as not achieved in both 2025 and 2026, with gaps remaining in two laws, and the by-laws are described as technically demanding and were not yet due. Adoption has been quick but alignment has twice fallen short, which does not support High.

RI-TEC-013 · North Macedonia

Broadband and high-capacity network coverage uneven

Technology and AI Digital infrastructure and connectivity

Small businesses and rural or non-urban areas face obstacles to fixed broadband, and high-capacity and 5G networks are still being rolled out.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission has repeatedly called for wider broadband access, and the Reform Agenda ties a payment to 5G roll-out and a 5G security by-law. The Commission reports continued 5G expansion, and a machine-translated national source gives 96.99% population coverage; 5G spectrum assignment and roll-out are validated as in_practice. The national broadband plan is validated as implemented, but its success is insufficient_evidence, and the national optical network is only proposed. The Commission reports household internet access rising to 90.8% in 2024, yet in 2025 it found that smaller companies and rural areas still face significant obstacles, and take-up of the fastest connections remains very low. Sources conflict on fixed coverage against the EU average. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    37 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    The Commission's wording has been largely stable. From 2021 to 2023 it repeated that there is a particular need to increase access to broadband and that smaller companies still face obstacles to fixed broadband. From 2024 it added fast internet for small businesses and non-urban areas and named rural areas alongside smaller companies. The 2024 Reform Agenda added a payment condition on 5G roll-out. In 2025 the wording hardened to significant obstacles for smaller companies and rural areas, while the 2026 assessment repeated the earlier sentence. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

    Adoption is not success.

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The latest EU items still find bottlenecks for rural areas and small businesses and ask the public broadcasting enterprise to strengthen its capacity to bring broadband to areas with limited commercial investment, while 5G continued to expand and the national optical network remains a plan. Sources conflict on the size of the gap, and both sides are cited: the ICT strategy gives 77% fixed coverage against an EU average of 78%, the Commission 79.6% against 93.1%, the strategy elsewhere 77% as very high capacity coverage after stating 69%, and the Broadband Competence Office's fast fixed coverage is 87.29% for 2024 in the 2025 report but 75% for 2025 in the 2026 report, a fall the report does not explain; household access figures (91.2% or 92% in 2025) measure take-up, not coverage, and do not settle this. What remains is fixed broadband for small firms and rural areas, very low take-up of the fastest connections and completing the 5G roll-out named in the Reform Agenda; the regional WiFi4WB hotspots do not name the country and cannot alone support a finding here.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    The Commission's sentence that smaller companies still face obstacles repeats from 2021 to 2026 with the same figures, so the default applies, though repeats are not independent evidence, and in 2025 the wording hardened to significant obstacles for smaller companies and rural areas. National averages did rise, with home internet access at 90.8% in 2024, 5G coverage at 76% in 2023 and 97% in a machine-translated 2025 national source, and some progress on ICT infrastructure in matching sub-area wording in 2025, while differences between earlier household figures reflect different measures, not conflict. No series tracks the rural and small-business gap itself, so the averages do not show that the unevenness has narrowed, and the chapter scale was not decisive.

  6. Comparator evidence Stated

    No comparator analysis for this issue in this run.

  7. Lesson Assessed

    No comparator analysis for this issue in this run.

  8. Priority Assessed

    ▲Priority High Validated

    Roll-out of 5G network and services is named in a Reform Agenda step, and the Commission repeats the particular need to increase access to broadband in its assessments from 2021 to 2026, which makes it central to the digital infrastructure theme. The payment condition covers the 5G part, not the rural and small-business part, which appears in repeated assessments and not in the chapter's key recommendations. The large volume of items on this issue, much of it repeated wording and national statistics, did not raise the rating.

    ◆Tractability Medium Validated

    Past progress is clear on 5G and on general access, where operators have invested and the Commission records continued expansion. The harder part depends on resources and on others: rural and low-demand areas lack commercial interest, the national network is at feasibility stage on a timetable to 2030 with mixed financing, and the government's own strategy, in machine translation, names lack of finance and high prices as challenges. Delivery therefore needs the ministry, the public broadcasting enterprise, operators and outside funders.

  9. Policy option Assessed

    No policy options for this issue in this run.

RI-TEC-015 · North Macedonia

Base registers incomplete, unreliable or not digitalised

Technology and AI Data and data governance Digitalisation of government or economic activity

Key registers, above all the population register, hold data of poor quality or are little used, and many institutional, property and intellectual property registers are not yet digitalised or kept up to date.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to complete the digitalisation of institutions' registers and data exchange, to improve the quality of population register data, and to digitalise intellectual property registration further. The Central Population Register is assessed as in practice: the Commission reported it operational in 2020 and used to cross-check the 2021 census. The Commission nonetheless found its use still limited in 2024, and the government's machine-translated 2025 strategy also describes it as underused and in need of a larger data set. The platform for digitalising registers, the Register of Registers and the digital register of charges are assessed only as proposed, and the 2023 strategy's baseline was no digital registers in 2022. The Commission still finds municipal property registers analogue. No outcome has been assessed. The gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    22 EU requirement items, 2021 to 2025.

    The Commission's focus has moved from the population register to registers in general. In 2021 it asked for population register data to be fully uploaded and checked and used to cross-check census data, and in 2022 and 2023 it asked for better data quality, continuously verified against other registers. From 2023 a key recommendation asks the country to complete the digitalisation of institutions' registers and data exchange as part of fully implementing the law on general administrative procedures, repeated almost word for word in 2024 and 2025. The 2025 report notes efforts but keeps the recommendation. The 2025 screening report adds intellectual property registration. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

Personal data protection law not aligned with EU rules

Technology and AI Data and data governance

The personal data protection framework is not fully aligned with the General Data Protection Regulation, the Law Enforcement Directive and the ePrivacy Directive, rules on international transfers are missing, and sector laws are not harmonised.

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align fully with the General Data Protection Regulation, to adopt a law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, to ensure safeguards for international transfers and to harmonise sector laws. The 2020 Law on Personal Data Protection has applied in full since August 2021, and the Agency reports supervisions and new rulebooks. A draft law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive was withdrawn in September 2022, and the Agency reports that neither that transposition nor its own draft amendments had started moving in 2025, in machine-translated reporting. In 2025 Parliament amended the law to allow transfers to NATO countries without prior consultation of the Agency, and the Commission found no progress and an insufficient framework. The validated assessment is that the gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is High (an analyst override) and tractability is Medium. In 2024 and 2025 the Commission records no progress and states that full alignment remains pending, and it adds ePrivacy alignment.   5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The 2020 law is proposed as in practice, with the Commission confirming full application from August 2021, while the amendments and the Law Enforcement Directive law are proposed only, the earlier draft was withdrawn in 2022, and all these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is full alignment with the General Data Protection Regulation, a law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, safeguards for transfers, harmonised sector laws and confirmed ePrivacy alignment. Sources conflict, since the State Audit Office and the Agency's strategy describe the law as aligned while the Commission calls the framework insufficient, and the country claims full ePrivacy alignment while the Commission seeks further efforts; this judgement does not rely on Article 122 of the unofficial translation, which may be mistranslated and, read literally, would suspend core chapters until accession.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    The Commission found no concrete progress on the Law Enforcement Directive in 2020, partial alignment and a need for full alignment in 2023, and pending alignment in 2024 and 2025, so the requirement has not changed across three or more reports. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2024 and 2025 covers more than this issue and was not decisive. The 2025 transfer amendment without equivalent safeguards is a further concern but a single event.

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its network and information security law with the NIS2 Directive and the Cybersecurity Act, to adopt and implement a cybersecurity strategy, and to improve coordination, and the Reform Agenda ties payments to the law and strategy, an operational competent authority and the NIS2 disclosure and crisis frameworks.   5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The NIS2-aligned network and information security law took effect in January 2026, a National Cybersecurity Council has been set up, and the 2026 report finds that the framework contributed to NIS2 alignment, but the Commission still asks for further alignment with EU cybersecurity rules and finds the law misaligned with NIS2 on personal data protection because the data protection agency's opinion was disregarded. No 2026 item for the country reports the by-laws, the entity lists or the disclosure and crisis frameworks as adopted, and the 2026 Communication's calls on cybersecurity concern all enlargement countries and do not alone support a finding here. What remains is the outstanding NIS2 provisions, including those on personal data, Cybersecurity Act certification alignment, the by-laws and entity lists, the disclosure and crisis frameworks, working coordination and application to the sectors deferred until accession; the law's text is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

    ↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

    Commission items moved from no further progress on the 2019 draft law in 2021, through repeated calls to adopt the law and strategy in 2022, 2023 and 2024, to adoption of the strategy in January 2025 and the law in June 2025, which the 2025 report counts as some progress. The chapter scale (limited progress 2021 to 2024, some progress 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and the improvement lies in the legal and strategic framework, since no item shows better coordination after the 2023 call, the 2024 audit finding of a Council that met once and the 2025 strategy's own description of coordination as critical. A February 2022 ITU item lists the law as existing while the Commission's 2022 report says it was still a draft, and later Commission and audit items support the draft reading; the differing dates for the Council (2019 or 2020) and the action plan's end (2027 or 2028) do not affect this value.

The issue is the legal base on which the rest of the cybersecurity theme rests. The rating rests on these EU requirements and not on the large number of national plan and audit items.

    ◆Tractability Medium Validated

    Much of what remains is drafting that the Ministry controls, and adoption followed within a year of the Reform Agenda step, which favours progress; against this, the first draft law stalled from 2019 to 2025, the Council barely functioned and no item shows the by-laws adopted after their deadline. Coordination needs many bodies, the strategy itself names political support and budget as key risks, and one reporting obligation to ENISA cannot be met outside the EU. Tractability is therefore higher for legal alignment than for coordination.

RI-TEC-023 · North Macedonia

Operational cybersecurity capacity of public institutions weak

Technology and AI Cybersecurity

The national incident response centre and state institutions lack staff, expertise and secure infrastructure, so government services and digital infrastructure remain exposed to attacks.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
▽Tractability Low Validated

The Commission asks state institutions to strengthen their cyber infrastructure and expertise and the national Computer Incident Response Centre to strengthen its staffing and operational capacity significantly, and the Reform Agenda ties payments to operational response teams, a staffed competent authority and a secure government network. North Macedonia adopted a cyber security strategy and action plan in January 2025 and a law on network and information security in June 2025, which establishes the national and government response teams. The State Audit Office reports, in machine-translated findings, that only 3 of 11 MKD-CIRT posts were filled and that 67% of surveyed institutions had no response team, and the disaster recovery centre is used by 3 of about 140 bodies. In April 2026 the Commission still reports major deficiencies. The validated assessment is that the gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is High and tractability is Low. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    29 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    From 2020 to 2023 the Commission frames cybersecurity mainly at regional level, as a priority for capacity building and resilience against hybrid threats. From 2023 its country wording is essentially unchanged: state institutions need stronger cyber capacity, infrastructure and expertise, and the national response centre needs more staff. The 2025 wording sharpens this to significant strengthening of the centre. In October 2024 the Reform Agenda adds concrete payment conditions on response teams, the competent authority and a secure network. The Commission's reform programme assessments move from large deficiencies in 2025 to major deficiencies in 2026. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The Commission still calls in 2026 for stronger infrastructure and cybersecurity expertise in state institutions and a substantial increase in the national response centre's staff and operational capacity, and its assessment of the economic reform programme reports major deficiencies in the security of digital infrastructure and government services. The 2026 report also records a response beyond paper, as the ministry established MKD-GOV-CSIRT for the executive authorities, investing in an incident response platform and staff capacity, alongside a new cybersecurity department and a National Cybersecurity Council, so the gap is no longer wholly open, although no item yet shows the team working to the Reform Agenda standard. What remains is a fully staffed national centre, trained and working response teams, security officers and tested plans in institutions, and secure government infrastructure in actual use; the audit evidence on institutions is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    The Commission's wording is essentially unchanged across three reports, that state institutions need stronger capacity and infrastructure and the national centre more staff (2023, 2024, 2025), and its reform programme assessments repeat large or major deficiencies in 2025 and 2026, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Incident counts cannot show a trend in capacity, because reporting was not mandatory and the figures are not comparable (1,441 or 1,443 for 2020, 2,804 for 2022, about 170 in 2023 on an unstated definition). The World Bank's advanced rating and the audit's finding of poor protection are a noted difference and not a conflict, since an index of national commitments and a test of practice measure different things, and the 2024 index itself lists technical and capacity measures as areas for growth.

  8. Priority Assessed

    ▲Priority High Validated

    Operational national and government CERTs, a staffed competent authority and a secure government network are Reform Agenda payment steps, and the Commission has repeated the need for capacity in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports. The Commission's reform programme assessments also name these deficiencies, and without operating capacity the legal framework has little effect, so the issue is central to the theme. The rating does not rest on the volume of audit and action plan items.

    ▽Tractability Low Validated

    Progress needs people the state has struggled to hire and keep (IT posts about half filled, 3 of 11 MKD-CIRT posts filled, a shortage the strategy says extends across the region), action across about 140 bodies, and budgets the strategy itself calls at risk, while the main infrastructure is at pre-feasibility stage and looks to outside funding. Past progress is weak, as most surveyed institutions had no response team five years after the previous strategy called for them, and the new 40% salary supplement is adopted with no item yet showing its effect. Strengthening MKD-CIRT alone would be more achievable than system-wide capacity, and the audit and strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to implement the EU 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox, including supplier risk assessment and restrictions on high-risk suppliers, and the Reform Agenda requires a fully implemented 5G security by-law by December 2027. April 2021 amendments gave the regulator prior security approval of 5G equipment, and the Commission reported the regulator adopted by-laws in 2022, but the screening report says not all the amendments were fully implemented. The 2025 Law on Electronic Communications, validated as adopted, empowers the regulator to assess suppliers and restrict high-risk ones, according to a machine-translated text. The 5G security by-law and the supplier risk assessment remain proposed, and no item shows an assessment carried out. No outcome is recorded. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    12 EU requirement items, 2021 to 2026.

    The Commission has named the 5G toolbox in successive recommendations from 2022 to 2025, and the core requirement has not changed. In 2024 the Reform Agenda turned it into a payment condition linked to a 5G security by-law and 5G roll-out. In 2025 the wording became more specific, asking the country to continue implementing the toolbox, including assessing suppliers' risk profiles and restricting or excluding high-risk suppliers. The Commission's 2025 enlargement communication also presents secure 5G infrastructure under the toolbox as a regional priority. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The latest EU items ask the country to continue implementing the toolbox, including assessing suppliers and restricting high-risk ones, and the Reform Agenda requires the security by-law fully implemented by December 2027; the 2025 law is proposed as adopted, the by-law and supplier assessment as proposed, and the 2021 amendments as reversed because the new law replaces them, all of which are proposals for review. What remains is adopting and applying the by-law and actually carrying out supplier risk assessments and any restrictions, since the law gives the power (machine translated, capped at Medium) but no item shows it used. The Reform Agenda's statement that the step is largely achieved sits against its own partial compliance baseline and the Commission's later wording, and it appears to rest mainly on spectrum and legislation, so it is not treated as closure; the Commission's finding that this law's reform step was not achieved concerns the Code and the Gigabit Act and not the toolbox, and the law allows 15 months for by-laws, so the finding does not decide this gap.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    The Commission has named the 5G toolbox in its recommendations in four successive reports (2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, two of these items being classified under the framework issue), and its November 2025 wording still asks the country to continue, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Legal steps did occur (2021 amendments, 2022 by-laws, the June 2025 law with supplier risk provisions), but the screening report says not all the 2021 amendments had been implemented. A reviewer could read the 2025 law as the start of improvement, but it began to apply only in June 2026 and no later EU item assesses it.

RI-TEC-026 · North Macedonia

Electronic identification and trust services not usable or recognised

Technology and AI Digital identity

Electronic identification and signature tools are costly, cumbersome and little used, qualified trust services are not widely available, and the country is not yet on the EU trusted list or in cross-border wallet arrangements.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

Under the Reform Agenda, the EU asks North Macedonia to join the EU Third Countries trusted list, make qualified trust services available, implement a Digital Identity Wallet and sign the Western Balkans mutual recognition agreement on trust services, and the Commission repeatedly finds the existing e-identification and e-signature tools not user friendly or free for citizens. The 2019 law is in practice, two providers accredited in 2021 offer advanced and qualified signatures, and the Ministry of Digital Transformation has supervised them. This provider outcome is assessed as a mixed success with Medium attribution. Electronic identity is in practice but little used, and the machine-translated audit found that high-level eID did not raise use. The country requested trusted list inclusion on 30 October 2025, but the Commission considers the step not achieved, and the wallet and cross-border recognition remain proposed. The gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    19 EU requirement items, 2021 to 2026.

    The requirement has grown from usage to recognition. In 2021 the Commission noted only that electronic signature use had increased modestly. In 2024 the Reform Agenda set payment conditions to join the trusted list, issue qualified certificates and implement a wallet and the regional agreement, and the annual report asked for alignment with the revised eIDAS Regulation and described the tools as cumbersome, not free and not user friendly. The 2025 report says the tools are "still" not user friendly or free. In May 2026 the Commission specified the outstanding trusted list tasks and set a grace period to 31 December 2026. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    Two providers offer advanced and qualified signature services, as the Commission reports and as the Reform Agenda step asks, but the same step is not achieved, the tools remain not free or user friendly, and the wallet and mutual recognition are still proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. The two sides conflict: North Macedonia reports the trusted list preparation complete and considers the step achieved, while the Commission says the self-assessment and published list are outstanding. What remains is inclusion in the trusted list (grace period to 31 December 2026), usable and free tools in common use, the wallet and cross-border recognition.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    The Commission said in 2024 that the tools were cumbersome and neither free nor user friendly, and in 2025 that they were still not, while its 2021 report recorded only a modest rise in electronic signature use. In 2026 it found the trusted list step not achieved despite the request of 30 October 2025, so steps were taken without a changed result. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive, and the 2024 audit evidence that high-level eID did not raise use is machine translated and capped at Medium.

    Joining the trusted list and implementing the wallet are Reform Agenda steps, the first with a stated payment provision, and the Commission repeated its concern about the tools in 2024 and 2025. Recognition and use are central to the electronic identification theme.

    ◆Tractability Medium Validated

    The outstanding trusted list tasks are specific and technical, and two providers have passed ministry checks, which favours progress. Use and usability need many institutions and users, the wallet depends on regional partners and the mutual recognition agreement, and the list depends on Commission assessment. The audit found failed procurement of institutional seal certificates (machine translated, capped at Medium), which is a warning on delivery.

RI-TEC-028 · North Macedonia

Interoperability platform and data exchange underused

Technology and AI Interoperability and electronic systems Data and data governance

Institutions do not use the national interoperability platform regularly, so administrative data are not shared ex officio between institutions, including for checks such as asset declarations and inspections.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to fully implement the law on general administrative procedures by completing data exchange, and a Reform Agenda payment condition asks for more data exchange between institutions and documents obtained ex officio. The interoperability platform is in practice, and the Commission reports that customs exchanges data regularly through it. Government figures, machine translated, show connections rising from 39 institutions in 2021 to 58 or 63 in 2025 and transactions reaching 8 million in 2024, with the Commission noting more connections and transactions. The Commission still finds only a few institutions using it, and the government's 2021 conclusions on connecting about 1,300 institutions are assessed as failed, with Low attribution, after the audit found only six new requests. The planned upgrade remains proposed. The gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    29 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2025.

    The diagnosis has hardly changed, while the requirement has become firmer. In 2020 the Commission found that many institutions did not use the system despite having the equipment, and asked for political will and funding. In 2021 and 2022 it asked for administrative data sharing to be reinforced and simplified, citing missing communications software and lack of will. From 2023 a key recommendation asks the country to complete data exchange under the law on general administrative procedures, repeated in 2024 and 2025, and in 2024 the Reform Agenda tied ex officio data exchange to a payment condition. Specific demands also appeared for asset declaration checks and inspections. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  4. Outcome Assessed
    • Government conclusions of June and September 2021 on connecting to the interoperability platform: ✗Success Failed ▽Attribution Low

    Adoption is not success.

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The platform operates and some institutions, such as customs, exchange data regularly, but the 2025 Commission recommendation still asks to complete data exchange and the responding upgrades and reforms are mainly proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. There is a confirmed contradiction: the country told the 2023 screening that the once-only principle is applied, while its 2024 Reform Agenda says institutions still do not gather evidence ex officio. What remains is regular use of the platform by the institutions obliged to use it, so that evidence is obtained ex officio as the law prescribes.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    Commission wording that few institutions use the platform runs from 2020 through 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, which sets the persistent default; the 2025 report records only efforts and repeats the requirement. Connection and transaction figures rose (39 institutions in 2021 to 58 or 63 in 2025; 1.5 million transactions in 2022 to 8 million in 2024), and the Commission confirms the increases in 2023 and 2024, but the counts come from government documents, machine translated and capped at Medium, and most institutions remain outside. The 2020 Commission 'slight increase' and the audit's falling traffic are a noted difference of measure and period, and the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.

  6. Comparator evidence Stated
    CMP-0004

    Moldova Draft country page

    What was done: Moldova put a legal duty and sanctions behind MConnect from January 2021, and the operator reports high volumes, but no evidence shows that the sanctions were applied or what changed use. A Court of Accounts page on MConnect was blocked and never read, and is a recorded gap.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia already has a legal obligation to use its platform, and its 2023 strategy says competence to inspect laws on ICT use is not established, so Moldova's sanctions may be the closest parallel in these cases. The evidence stops at the text of the law: it does not show that the sanctions were applied or that they raised use. If North Macedonia considered a sanction in law, this case could show only that such a mechanism exists on paper and is untested here, and that a connection count, such as 480+, may not show regular use.

    ◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

    CMP-0005

    Serbia

    What was done: Serbia has a 2016 legal duty to exchange data and a Bus to which the Commission says more databases are connected, but no source measures use by institutions. Around half of surveyed citizens still report being asked for documents the state holds.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Serbia does not show what raises institutional use, because no source text searched measures it. It suggests that a legal duty and a live exchange system, with more databases connected, may sit alongside about half of surveyed citizens reporting they were still asked for documents. If so, this would be relevant to North Macedonia's conflict between telling the screening that once-only is applied and its Reform Agenda saying institutions do not gather evidence ex officio. The lesson goes no further than this: connection and a review of sampled services may not settle whether evidence is obtained ex officio.

    ◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

    CMP-0006

    Montenegro

    What was done: Montenegro's register pairs in active exchange are reported as 18 and then 37 while institutions with access stay at 21, on government figures with no stated cause. The Commission still finds register integration and once-only incomplete, and an official says strengthening the inspection was not achieved because of staffing delays.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Montenegro gives two reported points on use, not a series: active register pairs of 18 and then 37 while institutions with access stay at 21, on unverified government figures, the later from a proposal text. No source text searched says why, although a new X-Road platform is reported in between. Its stated obstacles, data not available through web services and slow settling of legal and organisational preconditions, resemble North Macedonia's need to digitalise registers, change processes and integrate software. An official reports that strengthening the inspection was not achieved, and no extracted item shows whether it has acted on data exchange, so the case says nothing on inspection as a lever. If the figures hold, the case suggests that counts of connected institutions and of active exchanges may move separately.

    ◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

  7. Lesson Assessed

    Three points recur. First, a connection count does not show regular use. North Macedonia's own figures separate connected from active institutions, and Montenegro's government reports active register pairs rising from 18 to 37 while institutions with access stayed at 21. Second, a legal duty, even with sanctions, may sit alongside continued underuse or continued requests for documents: Moldova added fines and disqualification from 18 January 2021 with no evidence on use afterwards, and in Serbia about half of surveyed citizens still reported submitting documents the state holds, under a duty dating from 2016. Third, the stated obstacles are institutional: Montenegro names data not available through web services and slow legal and organisational preparation, which resemble North Macedonia's own reasons of IT staff, coordination, and register, process and software changes. A sanction does not supply any of these. Agent synthesis, validated at G6b

    No evidence recorded for this step in this run.
  8. Priority Assessed

    ▲Priority High Validated

    Data exchange and ex officio evidence sit in a Reform Agenda payment condition, and completing data exchange was a recommendation on public administration reform in 2023, 2024 and 2025, in the main findings in the last two. The 2026 key recommendations on public administration do not repeat it, but the payment condition stands and the 2026 report finds that poor interoperability between databases limits the verification of asset declarations, so the issue remains central to the interoperability and data themes. The large number of items, mostly from one national audit, played no part in this rating.

    ◆Tractability Medium Validated

    The platform exists and the government controls it, and use has risen somewhat, which favours progress. Against that, the audit found about 1,300 obliged institutions with no costed plan, IT pay at less than half the private sector and no coordinating body, findings the 2025 strategy partly repeats (all machine translated, capped at Medium), and the Commission cites missing software and lack of will. ITU's account of a ministers' council is a noted difference over a different body, leaving how far coordination worked in practice uncertain.

    RI-TEC-028Internal draft Agent synthesis

    Option 1: Measure use and ex officio evidence, not only connection

    Details
    Comparator it draws on
    Montenegro, Serbia
    Gap it addresses
    regular use of the platform by the institutions obliged to use it, so that evidence is obtained ex officio.
    Rationale
    Montenegro counts active register pairs as well as institutions with access, and Serbia's civil society monitor pairs a citizen survey on documents resubmitted with a review of sampled services. A source-stated point from the Serbian monitor, that compliance with the procedural duty needs monitoring, carries an item-level transferability judgement of conditional.
    Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
    Conditional: the measures are institutional and could be applied in North Macedonia, but none of the cases shows that measuring raised use.
    Problem it targets
    coordination failure (MEC-08) and the confirmed conflict between the country's statement that once-only is applied and its Reform Agenda's statement that institutions do not gather evidence ex officio.
    Preconditions
    an agreed definition of active use per institution and per register, and a body that collects it regularly; North Macedonia's own figures for 2025 differ (33 and 37 active institutions), which shows the need.
    Risks
    a new indicator that is reported but not acted on; government self-reporting without independent checks.
    Responsible actor
    the Ministry of Digital Transformation, which runs the platform and leads digitalisation projects, with the institutions obliged to use it. The body that oversees the Law on General Administrative Procedure is not identified in the evidence.

RI-TEC-029 · North Macedonia

Customs IT systems not aligned with EU electronic customs

Technology and AI Interoperability and electronic systems

National customs IT systems are not yet aligned with the EU electronic customs strategic plan, and upgrades such as the New Computerised Transit System phases, export and import control systems are delayed or understaffed.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to keep consolidating and upgrading its customs IT systems in line with the Union Customs Code work programme and the electronic customs strategic plan, to upgrade its transit system to Phase 6 and to recruit IT staff, and states that alignment on accession is critical to EU financial interests and security. After delays reported in 2023 and 2024, the Commission states that the New Computerised Transit System Phase 5 was completed and launched in January 2025, and notes good progress. Phase 6, the export system and the import control system remain Reform Agenda steps due between 2026 and 2027. The screening report rates alignment between low and partial, with remaining systems costed at about EUR 34.5 million. No usage data exist for Phase 5. The validated judgements are priority High, direction of travel improving, unresolved gap partly_addressed and tractability High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    27 EU requirement items, 2021 to 2026.

    The core recommendation has barely changed: from 2021 the Commission asks the country to consolidate and apply its customs IT systems in line with the strategic plan modules and ensure their upgrade, and from 2024 it adds the Union Customs Code work programme and continued legal alignment. The specific ask moved with events: implement Phase 5 in 2023 and 2024, then upgrade to Phase 6 in November 2025. In 2024 the Reform Agenda set payment conditions for Phase 6, the export system and the import control system, and staff recruitment became a recurring ask. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

The sub-area wording matches this issue, yet the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.

RI-TEC-036 · North Macedonia

National e-services portal limited in range and use

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services

The national e-services portal offers too few transactional services, is little used, or does not serve all users.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to offer many more fully digitalised services on its national e-services portal and to treat the digitalisation of public services as a priority, and a Reform Agenda payment condition requires a 50 per cent increase in the offer of e-services. The Commission states that the portal was upgraded, its offer widened with services most demanded by citizens, and some certificates put online. The State Audit Office, in machine translation, found only 0.556 requests per registered user and about 140 laws not aligned with the digitalisation package, and the 2025 strategy reports about 13 of 100 adults registered. In April 2026 the Commission found digital government quite underdeveloped, with most e-services rarely used. There is no outcome evidence. The validated judgements are priority High, direction of travel persistent, unresolved gap partly_addressed and tractability Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    117 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    The Commission's message has stayed essentially the same from 2020 to 2026. It first asked institutions to commit more to the portal and to encourage its use. From 2022 it asked for a wider offer of services and noted that fully electronic services had barely grown. In 2023 and 2024 it asked for the 135 new services to be completed and found the most common services, such as personal documents, still not online. From 2024 the Reform Agenda added the 50 per cent target, and in 2025 the screening asked for digitalisation to be treated as a priority. In 2026 the Commission still describes rare use and few fully transactional services. Agent synthesis, validated at G7
