  4. Outcome Assessed

    No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue.

    Adoption is not success.

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The Reform Agenda requires a 50% increase in e-services, and the Commission still finds in 2026 that service delivery requires efforts to meet EU standards, while the portal reached 338 services by the end of August 2026, including partly available ones, with usage doubled. Progress against the 50% target still cannot be fixed, because the 264 baseline conflicts with the Commission's 392 and 124 figures, and the 2026 report gives 338 services in one chapter and 336 in another. What remains is a much wider set of fully transactional, commonly requested services that people actually use, on an agreed count, and equal access: the 2026 report adds a requirement that digital public services meet accessibility standards and finds that digital divides leave rural and older women behind, while the Commission's statement that the portal caters for special needs still conflicts with the audit's finding (machine translated, capped at Medium) that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services.

    ↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

    From 2020 to 2025 the Commission repeated the same shortfall of too few fully transactional services, low use and below-expectation results, but its 2025 report recorded the most-demanded services and some certificates going online, and the 2026 report bears this out, finding significant improvements in digitalisation in 2025 and early 2026 and a portal usage rate that doubled from the previous year. The Commission's 2026 assessment of the economic reform programme still calls digital government quite underdeveloped, with most e-services rarely used; that describes the level rather than the change, and both are cited, so the improvement starts from a low base and service delivery still falls short of EU standards. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive, and service counts, including the 338 of August 2026, were not used for the trend because their definitions differ.

  6. Comparator evidence Stated
    CMP-0007

    Moldova Draft country page

    What was done: Moldova digitalised services through a long donor-backed project and assisted access, and reports online use rising, with service-level data for 2022 showing most digital services unused. The rise rests on agency and funder reporting, and no extracted item shows what caused it.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia's stated mechanism includes low uptake of a working portal (MEC-11), and the Commission's 2024 report gives 292,179 users and 2,070 monthly applications, with no reference period beyond 'currently'. If North Macedonia's position resembles Moldova's, a count of digital services would say little about use, since more than half of those reported for 2022 had no users, although 51 of the 128 had no demand on any channel. Moldova also reports use rising alongside service redesign and assisted access, but it does not show which measure raised it, so any of them would be a hypothesis to test.

    ▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

    CMP-0008

    Albania

    What was done: Albania placed most services on e-Albania, with a 2023 law obliging institutions to use it, and an international source reports high use. Full transactions are not established, payment often fails, and no extracted item shows that the law or the portal caused the reported use.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia's 2025 strategy proposes updating the law towards mandatory integration or connection of each e-service on the portal, and its stated mechanisms include coordination failure (MEC-08) and low uptake (MEC-11). Albania shows that a duty on institutions can sit alongside most services being placed on one portal and high reported use, but no extracted item shows that the duty caused either, and the legal e-payment duty is reported as limited in practice. If North Macedonia adopted such a duty, this case would not support expecting it to drive use; it supports, at most, the RCC's untested statement that uptake is linked to the portal's central role.

    ◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

    CMP-0009

    Montenegro

    What was done: Montenegro launched a new portal in December 2024 and a plan for transactional services, but sampled core services were not on it and use on the broad indicator fell before it launched. This case is too early and unverified, and its delivery figures rest on the government's own report.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Montenegro is the closest parallel to North Macedonia's position of a live portal, the most-needed services absent and capacity gaps, but its results are too early and unverified. It suggests a hypothesis, not a finding: a portal launched without the most-needed services on it may improve information without improving the service, which is the monitor's statement, drawn from seven sampled services, with grades that largely predate the first services. It also suggests that where a plan reports a delivered count, an independent check on whether services are transactional may be needed, given North Macedonia's own conflicting counts.

    ▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

  7. Lesson Assessed

    Three points recur. First, counts of digital services say little about use. In 2022 Moldova had 128 of 226 reported digital services with no users, although 51 of them had no requests on any channel. A Moldovan civil society source states that launch does not bring use, and this carries an item-level transferability judgement of conditional. Second, a portal without the most-needed services may improve information without improving the service: in Montenegro the monitor reports better information on the new portal while none of seven essential sampled services was on it. This matters because the Commission found that North Macedonia's most commonly requested services were not yet online. Third, a legal duty on institutions can sit alongside payment that often fails: Albania's law requires e-payment through the portal, but the monitor says users usually cannot pay. North Macedonia's 2025 strategy proposes a similar duty to integrate services on its portal. Agent synthesis, validated at G6b

  8. Priority Assessed

    ▲Priority High Validated

    The e-services increase is a Reform Agenda payment condition, and widening the portal's services is a recommendation repeated across three or more reports, including 'treat as a priority' in the 2025 screening. It is central to the digital government theme and Chapter 10. The rating rests on these, not on the large number of national audit and strategy items.

    ◆Tractability Medium Validated

    A single platform, EU funding and a dated payment step favour progress, and the Commission reports new services in 2025. Against that, the Commission's own wording shows the 135-service upgrade slipping for years and fragmented ownership, and the State Audit Office (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) reports about 140 laws unaligned and 101 of 242 posts unfilled, which means many institutions must act.

RI-FMW-002Validated

Work permits, quotas and residence conditions applied to EU workers

Chapter 2

EU EU workers and their family members are subject to work permits, annual quotas, residence permits or unspecified conditions (for example for seasonal work) that must be lifted or settled by accession. 14 EU requirements, 2023 to 2026.

→Direction of travel Persistent■Unresolved gap Open◆Priority Medium◆Tractability Medium

Permits and quotas are central to the chapter, but they are named as requirements only in the 2024 report and the screening report, not in the annual key recommendation, which is why this is central with thin support. If the reviewers read the key recommendation on non-discrimination as covering permits and quotas, this would be High; the large item count is mostly the law's own text and did not count.

RI-FMW-002 · North Macedonia

Work permits, quotas and residence conditions applied to EU workers

Chapter 2

EU workers and their family members are subject to work permits, annual quotas, residence permits or unspecified conditions (for example for seasonal work) that must be lifted or settled by accession.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission requires that, by accession, EU citizens can access North Macedonia's labour market without restrictions such as work permits, can reside for work without a visa or residence permit, and are specifically excluded from the annual quotas for foreign workers. The Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners has been in force since 2015 and was amended in 2021 and 2025, but the 2025 amendments only rename ministries and bodies. The Commission reports that the Employment Agency issues work permits under annual quotas, set at 10 000 for 2025. A law on seasonal work allows EU citizens access, but the Commission states that the conditions remain to be set in implementing legislation. Further amendments are listed only as proposals. The validated judgements are priority Medium, direction of travel persistent, unresolved gap open and tractability Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    14 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    The Commission's description of the regime has hardly changed: from 2020 its reports state that the country sets annual work permit quotas, and the 2024 and November 2025 reports repeat this. What changed is how explicit the requirement became. In 2024 the Commission asked only for further alignment of the Law on work and employment of foreigners. The February 2025 screening report then set out the requirement in full: no work permit, no visa or residence permit for work, and explicit exclusion from the quotas. In November 2025 the Commission added that the conditions for EU citizens in seasonal work remain to be specified. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  2. Country response Stated

    82 items, 2015 to 2026 on what the country has done.

  3. Implementation Assessed

    1 proposed · 3 adopted · 2 implemented · 2 in practice · 1 insufficient evidence

    10 interventions
    • Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners ●In practice
    • Law Amending and Supplementing the Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners 2021 ◐Adopted
    • Law Amending the Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners 2025 ◐Adopted
    • Proposed amendments on the employment of foreigners ○Proposed
    • Law on Foreigners ◐Adopted
    • 2019 amendments to the Law on Foreigners ◕Implemented
    • Single application procedure for work permits ◕Implemented
    • Annual quota of work permits for foreigners ●In practice
    • Law on the Work Engagement of Individuals adopted (proposed)
    • secondary legislation under the 2021 amending law ∅Insufficient evidence
  4. Outcome Assessed
    • 2019 amendments to the Law on Foreigners: ◐Success Mixed ◆Attribution Medium

    Adoption is not success.

    No evidence recorded for this step in this run.
  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ■Unresolved gap Open Validated

    What remains is access for EU citizens without work permits or residence permits, with their explicit exclusion from quotas, and no responding intervention is linked (statuses are proposals). The confirmed contradiction stands: the Commission says the law does not distinguish EU citizens, while the country says quotas do not apply to them under a reciprocity agreement. Art. 5(2) point 1 of the 2015 law (machine translated, so capped at Medium, and used under LIM-0024) partly explains this, because it does exempt foreigners given equality under such an agreement, but it is conditional, no item identifies a concluded agreement or shows it applied, and the Commission still requires the exclusion.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    The chapter scale is context only, since this is part of the chapter, but it bears on this issue: the Commission's rating moved from no progress in 2025 to limited progress in 2026, and it attributes the change to the Law on seasonal workers, which came into force on 1 January 2026. The State Audit Office reports that a working group formed in 2021 met only once and that no national AI strategy or legislation for public sector AI projects has been adopted. The audit reports that the ADA digital assistant is not functioning after about EUR 150 thousand was spent, and the strategy route and ADA are each assessed as failed. The Commission welcomed the signed AI Factory Antenna grant, but no activity under it is reported. Much of the national evidence is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence. The gap is assessed as open. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is new (as an EU requirement) and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ■Unresolved gap Open Validated

    Against the EU requirement of 2025 and 2026 to develop AI regulation and the governance and enforcement structures required by the AI Act, the 2026 report records only initial alignment work and preparatory steps to identify those structures. The signed Council of Europe convention, the adopted ICT strategy and the established AI Factory Antenna do not supply alignment or enforcement, and the national AI legislation and AI strategy remain plans, as national sources confirm (a machine-translated audit, capped at Medium). What remains is AI regulation aligned with the AI Act and an authority with the means to enforce it, none of which yet exists; the audit's statement that data protection law is aligned with the GDPR conflicts with the Commission's statement that full alignment is pending, and this is left unresolved.

    ●Direction of travel New Validated

    The EU requirement first appears in 2025, as an invitation to align fully with the AI Act, and the 2026 report restates it as developing AI regulation and the governance and enforcement structures the Act requires; two reports are too few for the persistent default, and the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. The 2026 report records first steps (initial alignment work including preparatory steps to identify those structures, signature in May 2026 of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, which the report does not say was ratified, and a national AI Factory Antenna), but these are preparatory and do not yet show alignment, so they do not support improving. National sources show the gap is older than the EU ask, so the value means new as an EU requirement, not new as a national gap.

    ◆Priority Medium Validated

    The rating rests on the EU layer: the AI requirement sits in body text in the 2025 and 2026 reports, is not a benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, and is absent from the Chapter 10 key recommendations of both years, which in 2026 name digital services, cybersecurity and digital trust but not AI. Repetition in two reports is short of the three the test asks for, so Medium reflects a requirement central to the AI theme with thin but growing support, and a third report repeating it, or its entry into the key recommendations, would support High. The much larger national audit, strategy and research evidence was given no weight.

    ◆Tractability Medium Validated

    Drafting is within government control, with the EU Act as a template, and the 2026 report records initial alignment work, signature of the Council of Europe convention and an AI Factory Antenna established under an EU grant signed in April 2026, which show that first steps can be taken. Enforcement structures still need a designated authority, specialist staff and funding across several bodies, and the earlier record is weak (one working group meeting since 2021 and a digital assistant no longer functioning, in machine-translated national evidence capped at Medium). The Commission also finds that the data protection agency cannot effectively police the increased use of AI and biometric data because of its limited oversight capacity.

RI-TEC-009 · North Macedonia

eHealth systems not interoperable or aligned with EU rules

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services Interoperability and electronic systems Data and data governance

Electronic health systems are not interoperable with health insurance data, referrals remain on paper, and the legislation is not aligned with the EU acquis on eHealth.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to make eHealth data interoperable with Health Insurance Fund data, to improve the eHealth appointment system and to align its legislation with the EU acquis on eHealth. The country runs the Moj Termin eHealth system, which the Commission says was introduced in 2013 and helped to significantly reduce waiting times, and it launched the MyHealth mobile application in 2023 and later added new modules. The Commission's statement on waiting times is judged as worked with Medium attribution, but it gives no figures. The Commission also finds that referrals were still on paper in 2024 and that the system is not yet interoperable with Health Insurance Fund data. Planned connections to the population register and the digital wallet remain proposed. The validated assessment is that the gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

    12 EU requirement items, 2022 to 2026.

    In 2022 and 2023 the Commission's wording is identical: Moj Termin should be extended to primary care doctors. The 2025 screening report adds a new element, stating that national legislation is not aligned with the EU acquis on eHealth. In November 2025 interoperability with Health Insurance Fund data is raised to a key recommendation, and the Commission adds that the appointment system needs to be improved. Functional upgrades in 2023 and 2025 are real but have not changed the stated shortfall. The default for three unchanged reports is not strictly triggered, and no Chapter 28 scale rating was decisive.

The Commission has found since 2021 that North Macedonia's Personal Data Protection Agency depends on government for staff and funds, and in 2025 said its capacities need to improve.   1. EU requirement Stated

    12 EU requirement items, 2021 to 2026.

    The Commission's concern has stayed the same in substance but its findings have become more severe. In 2021 it described the Agency's dependence on the Ministry of Finance and another ministry for recruitment and organisation. In 2022 and 2023 it said understaffing seriously harmed implementation, and in 2023 it called for alignment on the Agency's independence and noted that it is not financially autonomous. In 2024 it said the Agency lacks independence to hire staff and spend its budget. In 2025 it added that no director had been appointed and called for improved capacities, while a general communication asked for sustained resources and stronger independence. RI-TEC-019 · North Macedonia

Data protection authority not consulted and its advice not followed

Technology and AI Data and data governance

The data protection authority is not systematically consulted on sector and implementing laws, its recommendations are often not implemented, and parliament does not follow up its reports.

↓Direction of travel Worsening Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

In every report from 2020 to 2025 the Commission finds that the Personal Data Protection Agency is not systematically consulted on sectoral and implementing laws and that its recommendations are not fully followed, and in 2023 and 2024 that Parliament does not follow up its reports. In 2025 the Commission reported, as a concerning development, that the government removed the Agency from the list of bodies that must be consulted, and that Parliament amended the data protection law to allow transfers to NATO countries without consulting it. The Agency's own report, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, confirms the deletion in the Government's Rules of Procedure of 31 December 2024. The Commission found no progress on responsiveness to the Agency's recommendations in 2025. No intervention is recorded as responding to the issue. The validated assessment is open, with priority Medium, direction of travel worsening and tractability Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    16 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    The finding was stable in substance from 2020 to 2024, with small shifts in wording. In 2020 and 2021 the Commission said recommendations were not fully implemented and not all laws were submitted before adoption, noting some progress in 2021. From 2022 it said the Agency was not systematically consulted on sectoral or implementing legislation and its advice not always taken on board, and the 2023 screening report called for more systematic consultation. In 2023 and 2024 it added the lack of parliamentary follow-up and weak responsiveness. In 2025 the wording changed: the Commission reported the Agency's removal from the mandatory consultation list and no progress on responsiveness. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

What remains is systematic consultation of the Agency on sector and implementing laws, follow-up of its recommendations and follow-up of its reports in Parliament.

    ↓Direction of travel Worsening Validated

    The Commission's finding was essentially unchanged from 2020 to 2024, with some progress noted in 2021, and then changed in 2025, when the Government removed the Agency from the mandatory consultation list and Parliament amended the law without consulting it. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2025 matches this issue and the chapter scale was not decisive. RI-TEC-020 · North Macedonia

Weak compliance with data protection rules

Technology and AI Data and data governance Cybersecurity

Data controllers, including public bodies, do not apply data protection law in practice, breaches are frequent and not always reported, awareness is low, and sanctions are rare.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
▽Tractability Low Validated

The Commission finds that, in general, data controllers do not implement the Law on Personal Data Protection, calls for awareness raising in all sectors, and reports in 2025 that breaches are becoming more frequent, some go unreported and state bodies show low awareness. The law is assessed as in_practice, and the Agency reports 196 supervisions in 2025, with 121 decisions ordering violations to be removed. The Agency adopted a new rulebook on security of processing and took over an e-classroom platform, but the data protection officer network and the sanction amendments remain proposed. Success on awareness and on the e-classroom is insufficient_evidence, and no independent evidence shows changed behaviour. The Agency reports its Misdemeanour Commission disrupted by staff departures. Much Agency evidence is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence. The gap is assessed as open. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is persistent and tractability is Low. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    11 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    The Commission's concern has stayed the same while its findings have become broader. In 2020 it notes that misdemeanour fines for data protection breaches remain low. In 2023 it states more generally that controllers do not implement the law and that there is a strong need for awareness raising and a culture of data protection in all sectors. By November 2025 it adds that breaches are increasingly frequent, some are not reported as the law requires, and state administrative bodies still show low awareness and insufficient IT protection of personal data. Compliance has not been a named key recommendation in these reports. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ■Unresolved gap Open Validated

    The security rulebook has been adopted and an e-classroom is in place, but the data protection officer network and the sanction amendments are still only planned, no independent evidence shows changed behaviour, and the 2026 report again finds digital safeguards in state bodies insufficient and severe under-reporting of breaches. What remains is for controllers, including public bodies, to apply the law, report breaches and face effective sanctions. Two conflicts are reported and not resolved: reprimand counts differ between the Commission's report (10 for 2022, 17 for 2021) and the country presentation (4 for each), and the 2025 finding of increasingly frequent breaches conflicts with the 2026 finding of declining reported incidents, which low notification numbers (19 for 2022, 11 for 2025) and the Agency's under-reporting estimate do not settle.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    The Commission called fines low in 2020, found that controllers do not implement the law in 2023, found low awareness and more frequent breaches in 2025, and in 2026 still finds digital safeguards in state bodies insufficient, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale was not decisive. On breaches the reports conflict, and both are cited: the 2025 report finds breaches increasingly frequent and the 2026 report finds reported incidents declining, while the Agency's estimate of severe under-reporting, given in 2026, means neither figure shows whether compliance changed, so the conflict is reported and not resolved. Supervision counts measure enforcement rather than compliance, and the machine-translated Agency findings are capped at Medium confidence.

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its national interoperability framework and legislation with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act. North Macedonia stated at the 2023 screening that its framework was aligned with European Interoperability Framework 2.0 and that it planned further alignment with the updated version, and its 2025 digital strategy, in machine translation, says care will be taken to align. The State Audit Office found in 2022 that no study supported the ministry's claim to follow that framework. The alignment itself is rated proposed, and no aligned text is shown. The Commission links outdated legislation with under-use of the interoperability platform as an obstacle to digital services. The validated assessment is that the gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is Medium and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

The Commission asks North Macedonia to prepare several sectoral systems to connect with EU information systems, notably the civil protection system CECIS, the Business Registers Interconnection System (BRIS), EU taxation IT systems and the own resources reporting system. The Commission reported steps towards the CECIS connection from 2020 to 2022 but no progress in 2023, and says in 2025 that the link is still not made, while the country plans it by 2027. Some areas show more: the Commission states that alignment with the EU Digital COVID Certificate was completed in 2021 and that the country has achieved high-level integration of EU food safety IT tools. Most other responses are proposed, and BRIS and the Internal Market Information System also depend on EU decisions or accession. The validated assessment is open, with priority Medium, direction of travel persistent and tractability Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align with the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act, to align fully with electronic commerce rules and to harmonise its legislation with the Geo-blocking Regulation, and its screening report finds no alignment with the platform-to-business regulation. The Commission reports each year that citizens of only some Member States can use the European Health Insurance Card or access medical services in North Macedonia. Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services

The electronic public procurement system works, but some of its modules, such as the e-marketplace for low-value contracts and e-catalogues, are incomplete or little used by contracting authorities, and its data are not yet used for red-flag analysis.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to complete its e-procurement platform, build the confidence of contracting authorities to use the e-market for low-value contracts, and develop the red flag system and data analysis to report on possible corruption or bid-rigging. The Commission states that the electronic procurement system works efficiently and that its use is obligatory, and the system is assessed as in_practice. The e-market was launched in 2022, and the Commission reports 70 awards through it in 2022 and 258 in 2023. The Commission credits e-appeals and the electronic system with a high level of transparency, assessed as worked, though not with a fall in corruption. What remains is raising e-market use to the 800 awards set as a Reform Agenda payment condition for 2026, wider use of e-catalogues and stronger data analysis. The gap is assessed as partly_addressed. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is improving and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

In 2023 the focus turns to use: the Commission finds poor use of the e-market, little interest from procuring entities and e-catalogues only just starting, and asks for further development of the red flag system and data analysis. From 2024 the requirement becomes a quantified payment condition of at least 800 e-market awards in 2026, while the Commission repeats that the core system functions efficiently. RI-TEC-010 · North Macedonia

Digital communication with courts and justice system connections incomplete

Technology and AI Digitalisation of government or economic activity Digital government and digital public services

Digital communication with courts is incomplete, or justice system IT does not connect between institutions.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission has asked North Macedonia to digitalise its justice system, including digital communication with courts, videoconferencing for hearings and connections between justice IT systems. The Commission's 2026 Rule of Law report describes the digital interconnection of the Administrative Court, the Higher Administrative Court and other public bodies as a key advancement that enables electronic exchange of data and documents. Its implementation status is validated as implemented, but this rests on one statement with no usage data, and no outcome is recorded, so no result can be claimed. The Luris software, which North Macedonia said in 2023 needed connecting between the Ministry of Justice and the Public Prosecutor's Office, is at insufficient_evidence. The validated unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium, a tentative rating. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    6 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    The Commission's wording has narrowed over time. In 2020 it said that IT connections needed to be prioritised, including full digitalisation of cases and summoning, with training for judges and judicial staff. In 2023 it said that digitalisation, including interoperability between IT systems, and coordination between the relevant authorities needed to improve. In 2024 and 2025 it used identical wording, calling for more efforts to digitalise the justice system, in particular communication with courts and videoconferencing for court hearings. No Commission item from 2021 or 2022 is in the evidence. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

Broadband planning and investment framework incomplete

◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its national broadband targets with the Digital Decade, to align further with EU rules on aid for broadband deployment, and to strengthen the capacity of the public broadcasting enterprise mandated to build optical infrastructure. The National Operational Broadband Plan remains in force, but the Commission reported its implementation slowed in 2021 and further delayed in 2022. The country states that its targets will be aligned with the Digital Compass and that a mapping study is in preparation. A feasibility study for a national transport optical network has started, but no network is built. The Broadband Competence Office, in machine translation, reports that none of the three measures towards the 100 Mbps target was implemented. The validated judgements are priority Medium, direction of travel persistent, unresolved gap partly_addressed and tractability Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    12 EU requirement items, 2020 to 2026.

    In 2020 the Commission recorded some progress, citing ICT strategy preparations and the new Broadband Competence Office. In 2022 and 2023 its assessments found a strategic approach to broadband access lacking, the 2023 one adding national strategic investment and the targets of the National Broadband Plan. The 2025 screening made the requirement more specific: align the targets with the Digital Decade and align further on State aid for broadband, while noting that the Western Balkans Investment Framework and the Connecting Europe Facility had not been used for infrastructure. Newer Reform Agenda investment and a feasibility study are plans and do not yet show change, so this is not improving, and no 2026 Commission item addresses the framework. Sources conflict on the plan's period, with ITU and the 2025 report giving 2019-2029 and the 2022 and 2024 reports giving 2019-2023, which affects how far the delays can be measured against targets.

◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align further with Directive (EU) 2019/1151 on the use of digital tools and processes in company law, including scrutiny of a company's object and verification of the appointment and disqualification of directors. The country cites the Law on Trade Companies and the Law on Central Registry as regulating this area, both assessed as adopted. The Commission states that company registration and filing can be carried out fully online through the Central Registry's one-stop shop, which is assessed as in_practice, and it finds a high level of alignment with disclosure requirements and digital tools. No outcome has been assessed. What remains is the narrower set of legal amendments, with no draft reported. The gap is assessed as partly_addressed. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is persistent and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

The Commission states that data protection in the electoral sector needs improvement, that there is no assessment of whether the Electoral Code is harmonised with the data protection law, and that oversight of personal data used in election campaigns is inadequate. Amendments supplementing the provisions on biometric voter identification were adopted in April 2021, and the Commission notes that the Electoral Code brought in biometric data without prior consultation of the Personal Data Protection Agency. The amendments are assessed as adopted, and no item shows biometric identification used at an election. The Commission reports that the State Election Commission addressed some irregularities identified in supervision, but this does not reach the assessment of the Code or campaign data oversight. No evidence after 2023 addresses the issue. The validated judgements are priority Low, direction of travel insufficient_evidence, unresolved gap open and tractability Medium. RI-TEC-037 · North Macedonia

Sector and local online public services limited

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services

Online public services run by sector bodies or municipalities, outside the national portal, are limited in range, use or quality.

∅Direction of travel Insufficient evidence Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▽Priority Low Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission's requirement here is general: it states that ongoing digitalisation, including expanding services in sectors such as energy regulation and veterinary services, is essential to maintain progress. The Commission reports that the energy regulator, pharmaceutical chamber and pension insurance fund developed electronic services, and that the Cadastre Office's new digital services cut unresolved cases by 20% and the backlog by 10%; that result is assessed as worked with Medium attribution, for one period only. The national audit, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, describes five One Stop Shops, some not used effectively outside Skopje, portals requiring separate profiles and no public use statistics. A civil society study finds slow progress in municipal e-services. The validated assessment is partly_addressed, with priority Low, direction of travel insufficient_evidence and tractability Medium. In November 2025 it reported the Cadastre Office's new digital services. RI-FMW-014 · North Macedonia

Access and rights of third-country workers

Chapter 2

Workers from outside the EU face barriers to accessing the labour market, or their rights after admission are not protected or monitored.

∅Direction of travel Insufficient evidence Validated
∅Unresolved gap Insufficient evidence Validated
▽Priority Low Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

No Commission recommendation on third-country workers under Chapter 2 appears in the evidence, so this issue is raised mainly by international organisations, partly at regional level. They report an ageing population and skilled emigration that increase the need for foreign workers, alongside regulatory barriers to their immigration. For North Macedonia they report quota-based admission, passport retention, wage deductions of up to 30% and systematic underreporting of exploitation. They also describe permits tied to one employer and under-resourced, reactive labour inspection. No intervention by North Macedonia is linked to this issue and no outcome is recorded. The validated unresolved gap is insufficient_evidence and the direction of travel is insufficient_evidence. Priority is Low and tractability is Medium, the latter a provisional view. Comparators

Validated Comparator cases validated at G6b. The cases show what was tried, not what worked. Lessons are the tool's own reading across the evidence, validated by the analyst as conditional hypotheses; they are not stated by the sources.

Nationality discrimination in access to employment

Lessons across the cases Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Three points recur across the cases. First, two countries wrote rules for EU nationals as a separate regime inside a general foreigners law, giving equal treatment with nationals and work without a permit: Croatia in its 2011 Aliens Act and Montenegro in its December 2025 amendments. This answers the same legal mechanism the Commission names for North Macedonia, whose law treats EU citizens the same as other foreigners. Second, both countries deferred some or all of these provisions to accession, and no case shows that deferral is enough: Croatia's rating is not attributed to the Act, Montenegro's deferred clauses cannot yet have been applied, and Serbia reported a clause of this kind in 2015 while the Commission still found misalignment in 2015 and partial alignment in 2024 and 2025. Third, Serbia suggests that simplifying permits for all foreigners can earn a finding of limited progress while the difference in treatment the Commission names remains. No case addresses posts in private companies reserved for nationals, which is part of North Macedonia's gap.

CMP-0001

Croatia

What was done: Croatia wrote equal treatment and permit-free work for EU nationals into its 2011 Aliens Act, commencing on accession, and the Commission recorded completed legal alignment in 2012; no extracted item links the two. The extracted items give no data on what happened to EU workers in practice.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia's stated position is a foreigners law that makes no distinction for EU citizens, with a requirement that runs to the time of accession and further amendments of unknown content. If it chose to, North Macedonia could use a general foreigners law to carry a separate regime for EU nationals, adopted before accession, as Croatia did. Whether commencing that regime on accession would be enough is untested: the case does not show that this design earned the Commission's rating or that EU workers then had equal access, and it says nothing on reserved private sector posts.

▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

CMP-0002

Montenegro

What was done: Montenegro adopted a separate regime for EU nationals in its foreigners law in December 2025, with named clauses applying only from accession, and Chapter 2 was provisionally closed in June 2026; no extracted item links the two. What closed the benchmark is not public, and there are no measured results yet, only an uncorroborated Government claim of improved procedures.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: the Commission says North Macedonia's foreigners law does not distinguish EU citizens from other foreigners and that it needs to ensure unrestricted access by accession. On quotas its sources conflict: the Commission asks for EU citizens to be excluded, while the country's own account says quotas do not apply to them following a reciprocity agreement, as validated judgement JDG-009552 reports. If North Macedonia chose this route, it could write an equal-treatment clause and a quota carve-out into its foreigners law, as Montenegro did about six months before the chapter closed, with at least the carve-out deferred to accession. The sequence is suggestive only: it does not show that this law met the benchmark, that deferral was accepted, or that anything changed for EU workers.

▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

CMP-0003

Serbia

What was done: Serbia reported in the 2015 screening report that its 2014 law contains a clause giving EU citizens free access on accession, and it later amended the law to simplify permits, but the Commission still says EU citizens are covered by the rules for third-country nationals. This is a stalled case, and no extracted item says why.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Serbia is a stalled case with a closely similar Commission finding in different words, covering the permit regime but not reserved private sector posts. It suggests that if North Macedonia amended its foreigners law only to simplify permits for all foreigners, this could earn a chapter-level finding of limited progress while the gap the Commission names remains: permit simplification was one of two stated grounds in each year, with EURES preparations in 2024 and electronic data exchange in 2025. Serbia also reported a general ban on nationality discrimination in the same report that found misalignment, as North Macedonia does now in its own account. It cannot show why the gap persisted or whether a clause deferred to accession is enough.

◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

Full comparator brief

Interoperability platform and data exchange underused

Lessons across the cases Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Three points recur. First, a connection count does not show regular use. North Macedonia's own figures separate connected from active institutions, and Montenegro's government reports active register pairs rising from 18 to 37 while institutions with access stayed at 21. Second, a legal duty, even with sanctions, may sit alongside continued underuse or continued requests for documents: Moldova added fines and disqualification from 18 January 2021 with no evidence on use afterwards, and in Serbia about half of surveyed citizens still reported submitting documents the state holds, under a duty dating from 2016. Third, the stated obstacles are institutional: Montenegro names data not available through web services and slow legal and organisational preparation, which resemble North Macedonia's own reasons of IT staff, coordination, and register, process and software changes. A sanction does not supply any of these.

CMP-0004

Moldova Draft country page

What was done: Moldova put a legal duty and sanctions behind MConnect from January 2021, and the operator reports high volumes, but no evidence shows that the sanctions were applied or what changed use. A Court of Accounts page on MConnect was blocked and never read, and is a recorded gap.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia already has a legal obligation to use its platform, and its 2023 strategy says competence to inspect laws on ICT use is not established, so Moldova's sanctions may be the closest parallel in these cases. The evidence stops at the text of the law: it does not show that the sanctions were applied or that they raised use. If North Macedonia considered a sanction in law, this case could show only that such a mechanism exists on paper and is untested here, and that a connection count, such as 480+, may not show regular use.

◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

CMP-0005

Serbia

What was done: Serbia has a 2016 legal duty to exchange data and a Bus to which the Commission says more databases are connected, but no source measures use by institutions. Around half of surveyed citizens still report being asked for documents the state holds.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Serbia does not show what raises institutional use, because no source text searched measures it. It suggests that a legal duty and a live exchange system, with more databases connected, may sit alongside about half of surveyed citizens reporting they were still asked for documents. If so, this would be relevant to North Macedonia's conflict between telling the screening that once-only is applied and its Reform Agenda saying institutions do not gather evidence ex officio. The lesson goes no further than this: connection and a review of sampled services may not settle whether evidence is obtained ex officio.

◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

CMP-0006

Montenegro

What was done: Montenegro's register pairs in active exchange are reported as 18 and then 37 while institutions with access stay at 21, on government figures with no stated cause. The Commission still finds register integration and once-only incomplete, and an official says strengthening the inspection was not achieved because of staffing delays.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Montenegro gives two reported points on use, not a series: active register pairs of 18 and then 37 while institutions with access stay at 21, on unverified government figures, the later from a proposal text. No source text searched says why, although a new X-Road platform is reported in between. Its stated obstacles, data not available through web services and slow settling of legal and organisational preconditions, resemble North Macedonia's need to digitalise registers, change processes and integrate software. An official reports that strengthening the inspection was not achieved, and no extracted item shows whether it has acted on data exchange, so the case says nothing on inspection as a lever. If the figures hold, the case suggests that counts of connected institutions and of active exchanges may move separately.

◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

Full comparator brief

National e-services portal limited in range and use

Lessons across the cases Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Three points recur. First, counts of digital services say little about use. In 2022 Moldova had 128 of 226 reported digital services with no users, although 51 of them had no requests on any channel. A Moldovan civil society source states that launch does not bring use, and this carries an item-level transferability judgement of conditional. Second, a portal without the most-needed services may improve information without improving the service: in Montenegro the monitor reports better information on the new portal while none of seven essential sampled services was on it. This matters because the Commission found that North Macedonia's most commonly requested services were not yet online. Third, a legal duty on institutions can sit alongside payment that often fails: Albania's law requires e-payment through the portal, but the monitor says users usually cannot pay. North Macedonia's 2025 strategy proposes a similar duty to integrate services on its portal.

CMP-0007

Moldova Draft country page

What was done: Moldova digitalised services through a long donor-backed project and assisted access, and reports online use rising, with service-level data for 2022 showing most digital services unused. The rise rests on agency and funder reporting, and no extracted item shows what caused it.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia's stated mechanism includes low uptake of a working portal (MEC-11), and the Commission's 2024 report gives 292,179 users and 2,070 monthly applications, with no reference period beyond 'currently'. If North Macedonia's position resembles Moldova's, a count of digital services would say little about use, since more than half of those reported for 2022 had no users, although 51 of the 128 had no demand on any channel. Moldova also reports use rising alongside service redesign and assisted access, but it does not show which measure raised it, so any of them would be a hypothesis to test.

▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

CMP-0008

Albania

What was done: Albania placed most services on e-Albania, with a 2023 law obliging institutions to use it, and an international source reports high use. Full transactions are not established, payment often fails, and no extracted item shows that the law or the portal caused the reported use.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia's 2025 strategy proposes updating the law towards mandatory integration or connection of each e-service on the portal, and its stated mechanisms include coordination failure (MEC-08) and low uptake (MEC-11). Albania shows that a duty on institutions can sit alongside most services being placed on one portal and high reported use, but no extracted item shows that the duty caused either, and the legal e-payment duty is reported as limited in practice. If North Macedonia adopted such a duty, this case would not support expecting it to drive use; it supports, at most, the RCC's untested statement that uptake is linked to the portal's central role.

◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

CMP-0009

Montenegro

What was done: Montenegro launched a new portal in December 2024 and a plan for transactional services, but sampled core services were not on it and use on the broad indicator fell before it launched. This case is too early and unverified, and its delivery figures rest on the government's own report.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Montenegro is the closest parallel to North Macedonia's position of a live portal, the most-needed services absent and capacity gaps, but its results are too early and unverified. It suggests a hypothesis, not a finding: a portal launched without the most-needed services on it may improve information without improving the service, which is the monitor's statement, drawn from seven sampled services, with grades that largely predate the first services. It also suggests that where a plan reports a delivered count, an independent check on whether services are transactional may be needed, given North Macedonia's own conflicting counts.

▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

Draft policy options

Internal draft These options were signed off at G7 as internal drafts. They are not validated recommendations and have not been prepared for an external audience. Each rests on a validated unresolved gap and on comparator lessons that are agent synthesis, rated conditional. None is proposed because another country adopted it, and none is shown by the evidence to work.

Nationality discrimination in access to employment

RI-FMW-001Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 1: Write equal treatment for EU nationals into the law, as a distinct regime

Details
Comparator it draws on
Croatia, Montenegro
Gap it addresses
the law on access to the labour market does not give EU workers equal treatment with nationals.
Rationale
Croatia (relevance High) and Montenegro (relevance High) each placed EU nationals in a separate regime within their foreigners law, with equal treatment and permit-free work.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: the design answers the same mechanism, but neither case shows that it earned the Commission's assessment or changed access for EU workers.
Problem it targets
legal or regulatory gap (MEC-01).
Preconditions
North Macedonia has a separate law on employment of foreigners, so the regime would need to cover that law as well as any residence rules, not one act only; the provisions to be changed would first need to be listed.
Risks
drafting a clause that the Commission does not accept as full alignment, as in Serbia; leaving the reserved private sector posts untouched, since no case covers them.
Responsible actor
the Government, through the ministry responsible for the law on employment of foreigners, now the Ministry of Economy and Labour, with adoption by the Assembly.
RI-FMW-001Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 2: Settle the commencement design early, rather than assume that deferral to accession is enough

Details
Comparator it draws on
Croatia, Montenegro, Serbia
Gap it addresses
the requirement that EU citizens can access the labour market without restrictions by accession.
Rationale
all three cases. Croatia and Montenegro deferred provisions to accession, and Serbia reported a deferred clause while misalignment findings continued.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: this is a warning drawn from the tool's reading of three cases, not a tested lesson, and what closed Montenegro's benchmark is not public.
Problem it targets
legal or regulatory gap (MEC-01).
Preconditions
a clear view, through the negotiation process, of which provisions must apply before accession and which may start on accession.
Risks
a law that is aligned on paper but leaves EU workers inside the foreigner regime until accession, which may not satisfy a closing benchmark.
Responsible actor
the Government and its negotiating structures, with the ministry responsible for labour.
RI-FMW-001Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 3: Do not treat permit simplification or the general non-discrimination rule as the answer

Details
Comparator it draws on
Serbia
Gap it addresses
the Commission's finding that EU citizens are treated as any other foreigner. North Macedonia points to the reference to nationality discrimination in its Law on Labour Relations, but the validated gap judgement finds that this, being the country's own account, does not close the gap.
Rationale
Serbia (relevance Medium) simplified permits for all foreigners and reported a general non-discrimination clause, while the Commission still found that EU citizens were covered by the rules for third-country nationals.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: the point rests on the Commission's wording, not on a stated lesson, and Serbia's reasons for its slow pace are not in the evidence.
Problem it targets
legal or regulatory gap (MEC-01).
Preconditions
any permit reform would be paired with an explicit provision on EU nationals, as in Option 1.
Risks
reporting progress on procedures while the gap the Commission names remains.
Responsible actor
the ministry responsible for labour, and the Employment Service Agency where permit procedures change.

Related step outside the comparator evidence. Removing posts in private companies reserved for nationals is part of the gap but is not covered by any case, so no option is drafted on it here. The laws that reserve these posts are not identified in the evidence, and identifying them is an open question for the next run.

Interoperability platform and data exchange underused

RI-TEC-028Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 1: Measure use and ex officio evidence, not only connection

Details
Comparator it draws on
Montenegro, Serbia
Gap it addresses
regular use of the platform by the institutions obliged to use it, so that evidence is obtained ex officio.
Rationale
Montenegro counts active register pairs as well as institutions with access, and Serbia's civil society monitor pairs a citizen survey on documents resubmitted with a review of sampled services. A source-stated point from the Serbian monitor, that compliance with the procedural duty needs monitoring, carries an item-level transferability judgement of conditional.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: the measures are institutional and could be applied in North Macedonia, but none of the cases shows that measuring raised use.
Problem it targets
coordination failure (MEC-08) and the confirmed conflict between the country's statement that once-only is applied and its Reform Agenda's statement that institutions do not gather evidence ex officio.
Preconditions
an agreed definition of active use per institution and per register, and a body that collects it regularly; North Macedonia's own figures for 2025 differ (33 and 37 active institutions), which shows the need.
Risks
a new indicator that is reported but not acted on; government self-reporting without independent checks.
Responsible actor
the Ministry of Digital Transformation, which runs the platform and leads digitalisation projects, with the institutions obliged to use it. The body that oversees the Law on General Administrative Procedure is not identified in the evidence.
RI-TEC-028Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 2: Address the institutional preconditions before relying on enforcement

Details
Comparator it draws on
Moldova, Montenegro
Gap it addresses
as in Option 1.
Rationale
Montenegro's stated obstacles of data not available through web services and unsettled legal and organisational arrangements (CMP-0006), and Moldova's case, where a sanction was added without evidence that it supplied capacity or raised use.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: the obstacles are institutional and resemble North Macedonia's, but scale and starting point differ, and the Montenegrin figures are unverified. An item-level judgement on a Montenegrin source, that capacity must be tackled along with the technology, is also conditional and rests on a source rated Low.
Problem it targets
coordination failure (MEC-08) and insufficient resources (MEC-09).
Preconditions
a costed plan for connecting the obliged institutions, which the State Audit Office found missing for about 1,300 institutions, and filled IT posts.
Risks
the plan is drafted but not funded; staff outflow continues.
Responsible actor
the Government and the Ministry of Digital Transformation, with the institutions that hold the registers.
RI-TEC-028Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 3: Consider an enforcement mechanism for the duty to use the platform, as an untested option

Details
Comparator it draws on
Moldova
Gap it addresses
as in Option 1. North Macedonia already has a legal duty to use the platform, and its 2023 strategy says there is no accountability without an ICT inspection competence; both are machine translated.
Rationale
Moldova's fines and temporary disqualification for refusing data or asking for documents available on the platform.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional and untested: no source shows that the sanctions were applied or that they raised use.
Problem it targets
weak enforcement or oversight (MEC-04), which is not among the mechanisms recorded for this issue, so this option goes beyond the validated issue definition and is offered for discussion only.
Preconditions
Options 1 and 2 in place, so that a duty can be met and breaches can be seen.
Risks
sanctioning institutions that lack the staff and software to comply; enforcement on paper only.
Responsible actor
the Government and the Assembly for any change to the law, and a body given the inspection competence.

National e-services portal limited in range and use

RI-TEC-036Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 1: Agree one service-by-service count, with use, and repeat it

Details
Comparator it draws on
Moldova, Montenegro
Gap it addresses
the missing agreed count of fully transactional services, on which progress against the Reform Agenda target of a 50% increase cannot be fixed, because the government's baseline conflicts with the Commission's figures.
Rationale
Moldova's 2022 count, made service by service and separating fully from partly digital services, showed the gap between availability and use, though it was not repeated and Moldova's counts still differ. Montenegro suggests that a delivered count may need an independent check on whether services are transactional.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: a count could help settle North Macedonia's conflicting figures if repeated, but neither case shows that it did so.
Problem it targets
low uptake of systems already in place (MEC-11), and unreliable data on what exists.
Preconditions
a shared definition of a fully transactional service, agreed with the Commission for the Reform Agenda, and data on use per service.
Risks
a count produced once for a payment condition and then dropped; a definition loose enough to inflate progress.
Responsible actor
the Ministry of Digital Transformation, which leads digitalisation projects, with the institutions that own the services.
RI-TEC-036Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 2: Put the most-requested services online in full before widening the range

Details
Comparator it draws on
Moldova, Montenegro
Gap it addresses
the much wider set of fully transactional, commonly requested services that people use.
Rationale
Montenegro (relevance High), where a portal without the most-needed services improved information only, and Moldova, where many digital services had no users. A Moldovan source states that building without beneficiaries' views harms use; its item-level transferability is conditional, on user involvement in design, a condition the evidence does not show North Macedonia meets.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: Montenegro's portal is newer than North Macedonia's, so results at its stage may not predict results at a later one.
Problem it targets
low uptake (MEC-11) and weak administrative capacity (MEC-03).
Preconditions
a list of the most-requested services and their owners, which North Macedonia's strategy plans as an action but does not show delivered.
Risks
the selected services depend on registers and data exchange that are not ready, which ties this option to the interoperability issue (RI-TEC-028).
Responsible actor
the Ministry of Digital Transformation with the service-owning ministries and agencies.
RI-TEC-036Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 3: Pilot assisted access and measure its effect on use

Details
Comparator it draws on
Moldova
Gap it addresses
use of the portal and equal access, including the State Audit Office's finding that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services.
Rationale
Moldova reports use rising alongside service redesign and assisted access through its service centres, but does not show which measure raised it. North Macedonia so far plans only an analysis for DigInfo centres.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: the effect of assisted access is unmeasured in Moldova, so it transfers only as an idea to test.
Problem it targets
low uptake (MEC-11).
Preconditions
a measure of use set before the pilot starts; accessibility treated as a separate requirement, since assisted access does not by itself meet it.
Risks
centres that help people with information but not with completing services; cost without evidence of effect.
Responsible actor
the Ministry of Digital Transformation, which has said it will carry out the DigInfo analysis.
RI-TEC-036Internal draft Agent synthesis

A warning rather than an option: a legal duty to integrate services will not by itself raise use

Details
Comparator it draws on
Albania
Rationale
North Macedonia's 2025 strategy proposes making integration of e-services on the portal mandatory. Albania (relevance Medium) shows such a duty alongside most services on one portal and high reported use, but no source shows that the duty caused either, and payment through the portal often fails.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: if North Macedonia adopts such a duty, the comparator evidence supports pairing it with working payment and signature and with the resources the lead ministry lacks, not expecting it to drive use on its own.

Evidence and limits

Validated From the coverage and limits report signed off at G7.

Source coverage Agent synthesis

The run met most of its core source requirements for North Macedonia, but with gaps that matter for particular issues. Of 34 requirements, 16 were found, 13 partly found, 3 not found and 2 remain open. The main gaps are the National Programme for the Adoption of the Acquis, for which no version from 2020 onwards could be retrieved; opening or closing benchmarks for Chapter 2, which do not exist because no cluster has been opened; dedicated monitoring of the rights of foreign workers; and the SIGMA and OECD reports, whose publishers block automated download and which were not added by hand. Of 112 registered North Macedonia sources, 99 were available and 13 inaccessible. A large share of the evidence on the country response comes from Macedonian-language government sources and is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence. The comparator pilot used public sources only, with restricted EU documents and blocked sources recorded as gaps (LIM-0028), and extended machine translation to named comparator sources (LIM-0030). Refresh with the 2026 Enlargement Package (decision E18, 5 November 2026). Three Commission documents published on 4 November 2026 were added under the existing requirements for annual reports and the enlargement communication: the 2026 report, the factsheet (which held no in-scope claim) and the 2026 Communication. They bring the North Macedonia sources to 115, of which 102 are available, and add 155 in-scope items, none machine translated, so the share of machine-translated items falls slightly. The limit recording that the package was awaited (LIM-0036) is superseded; the exclusion of the Commission communication on preparing for a wider Union (LIM-0037) is kept, and its review point is met because the 2026 Communication repeats the regional roaming point. The refresh used the run's own rule versions and re-judged only the 41 issues the new items touch; evidence confidence, relevance and implementation statuses for the new material are proposals for the refresh G7.

Evidence limit 1,714 of 4,104 in-scope North Macedonia evidence items (42%) are machine translated, and their evidence confidence is capped at Medium. Source quality, evidence confidence and relevance are kept as separate judgements and never combined.

Methodological limitations Agent synthesis

The alpha found these limitations, each recorded in the alpha learning log. Extraction missed about one in eight in-scope claims in EU sources, mostly of low importance (LIM-0025, ALN-0017), and the second-pass check may have been applied unevenly between EU and other sources (ALN-0022). The automatic quote check confirms that a quote exists at its location, not that it is cut to the claim (ALN-0013). Only exact file duplicates are detected, so two versions of one screening report were counted twice until an independent check found them (ALN-0023). Parallel agents applied rules differently where the rules were silent, and judged priority inconsistently until a calibration across all issues (ALN-0012, ALN-0026). Agent inputs that were truncated or filtered by issue tag hid relevant evidence in two places (ALN-0025, ALN-0029). In the comparator pilot, first drafts of the cases contained serious errors that routine validation did not catch (ALN-0028), sources stated few lessons, so the case-level lessons are the tool's synthesis (ALN-0031, E15), and passing gates under a standing instruction moved the discovery of a language-limit problem to the end of the pilot (ALN-0030). Since decision E12, no person has read the source documents behind the extraction or the comparator cases; the checks were made by independent agents. Some validated judgement reasons still carry stage 10 wording, such as statuses described as proposals; the values were validated at G6.

Active limits for this run (28)
  • North Macedonia (MKD) only; comparator evidence only for the 2 to 3 issues selected for run 1b LIM-0008
  • Run 1 covers all of Chapter 2 (Freedom of movement for workers) plus the technology and AI theme: recommendations materially relating to the areas in taxonomy/themes.csv wherever they occur; incidental references to technology are out of scope; the full analytical chain is followed for every issue originating from an in-scope Chapter 2 item or technology and AI recommendation LIM-0009
  • Material outside Chapter 2 and the technology and AI theme is out of scope unless it is needed to follow the analytical chain of an issue already in scope; there is no list of deferred chapters LIM-0010
  • Evidence from 2020-01-01 to the evidence freeze date; earlier material only by logged exception where needed to understand the origin or evolution of an in-scope issue LIM-0011
  • English primary; Macedonian or Albanian only for core relevant sources with no suitable English version; each such source recorded in the register; machine translation flagged and capped at Medium confidence LIM-0012
  • No interactive dashboard in run 1 (no country or thematic views); a single static read-only review page (index.html) surfaces validated material and labelled work in progress; outputs remain internal analyst products LIM-0013
  • No National Programme for the Adoption of the Acquis (2020 or later) or its implementation reports: the Secretariat for European Affairs site had an expired TLS certificate and no copy was found elsewhere LIM-0014
  • No official national material on the European Health Insurance Card or the electronic exchange of social security information (EESSI): the Health Insurance Fund site blocks automated access LIM-0015
  • Documents blocked by publishers for automated download are not retrieved manually in the alpha: SIGMA 2021 and 2024, OECD Competitiveness Outlook 2024 and Labour Migration 2022, UNDP Digital Readiness Assessment, IOM migration profile, two Metamorphosis monitoring reports, the 16th SA Council press statement, State Audit Office originals (ministry copies used) LIM-0016
  • Research and civil society coverage of Chapter 2 is thin: one think tank study (MKD-RES-2023-001), evaluation highlights only (MKD-RES-2026-001) and one human rights report (MKD-CSO-2024-001) LIM-0017
  • Almost all national government sources are in Macedonian only (some bilingual with Albanian); evidence on the country response will mostly rely on machine translation capped at Medium confidence LIM-0018
  • Logged exception to the time window: the 2015 Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners (MKD-GOV-2015-001) may be used only where needed to understand the 2021 and 2025 amendments (MKD-GOV-2021-001, MKD-GOV-2025-001) LIM-0019
  • Claims mainly about events before 2020 are kept only as controlled exceptions where needed to explain an in-scope issue; each is flagged out_of_window with the reason and listed for the analyst. Current claims that refer back to earlier events are in scope LIM-0021
  • Digital skills are not part of the technology and AI theme; included only where directly linked to an in-scope technology or AI recommendation LIM-0022
  • Chapter 2 is read in its EU meaning: rights and access of EU and foreign workers in North Macedonia, labour-market access, equal treatment, EURES, the European Labour Authority, social security coordination, EHIC and anti-corruption measures tied to Chapter 2; emigration, brain drain and diaspora only where directly linked; nationals' access to EU labour markets and general labour-market policy out of scope LIM-0023
  • Extends the exception in LIM-0019 to Art. 5(2) point 1 of the 2015 Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners (MKD-GOV-2015-001), the only provision naming the EU, because a confirmed contradiction on quotas turns on it LIM-0024
  • About one in eight in-scope claims may be missed in EU sources, mostly of low importance (37 against 272 items in four sampled sources; the 8 of higher importance added). Long action plans and laws were screened by keyword and section, not read line by line LIM-0025
  • Comparator evidence is gathered for three named issues only (RI-FMW-001, RI-TEC-028, RI-TEC-036), as a deliberate expansion approved at G6, with no full country model LIM-0026
  • Logged exception to the time window: comparator documents from 2007 onwards on RI-FMW-001 only, for Croatia, whose reform predates accession in 2013, and Serbia's screening report LIM-0027
  • Comparator evidence uses public sources only. Restricted EU documents are not used, including the EU common position on Montenegro Chapter 2 (AD 26/26), so what closed that benchmark is known only from public statements. Blocked sources, including the SIGMA 2024 reports, are recorded as gaps and not retrieved manually LIM-0028
  • Comparator legal texts in Croatian, Serbian, Montenegrin or Romanian may be used where no English version exists; they are machine-translated and capped at Medium confidence LIM-0029
  • Extends LIM-0029 beyond legal texts to named machine-translated comparator sources: the Moldovan Court of Accounts reports (MDA-GOV-2024-001, MDA-GOV-2024-003), Montenegrin government reports (MNE-GOV-2025-002, MNE-GOV-2025-003, MNE-GOV-2026-003) and the explanatory statement in a Croatian bill (HRV-GOV-2023-002); and to English legal texts available only for payment (the Croatian Aliens Act). All capped at Medium confidence and labelled as such in every output LIM-0030
  • No person read the source documents behind the extraction or the comparator cases; extraction, classification and case checks were made by independent agents (E12), with measured error rates reported at each gate LIM-0031
  • All analytical judgements were validated by one person, the analyst, as sole decision-maker for the alpha (E13); no second reviewer validated priority, gaps or policy options LIM-0032
  • Some validated judgement reasons carry stage 10 wording or rest on mislabelled items, and seven judgements carry rereview_flag (GATE-0012); outputs show the reasons as validated, with a caveat LIM-0033
  • Comparator lessons and case-level transferability are agent synthesis, not stated by sources; the cases show what was tried, not what worked, so draft policy options are design options and warnings, not proven routes LIM-0034
  • Reform issues are derived from EU requirements, so problems raised only by national or independent sources fit no issue, and issues on themes with thin EU coverage, such as AI, rest on few EU items LIM-0035
  • The Commission communication "Preparing for a wider Union" and its staff working document on pre-enlargement policy reviews (6 October 2026) are not registered: they review the EU's own policies and budget and do not assess North Macedonia (clear-cut exclusion, country scope; to be surfaced at the refresh G6) LIM-0037
